# Introduction

## A book about earning autonomy

An AI agent becomes useful when it can complete a worthwhile task under conditions that someone can explain, measure, and control. A persuasive conversation is part of that experience, but it is only one part. The agent must obtain the right evidence, select appropriate tools, respect organizational authority, recover cleanly from interruption, and leave a result that a person or downstream service can verify independently of the model's prose.

This book follows those responsibilities from a first local prototype to a production release decision. Its central argument is straightforward: greater autonomy should follow demonstrated competence, explicit permissions, and recoverable execution. A system earns a wider action scope by performing reliably on representative tasks, staying within hard resource budgets, and remaining legible when it fails. A system prompt that tells a language model to act as a senior specialist cannot establish that competence by itself.

Across the industry, teams have discovered a recurring tension between rapid generation and operational accountability. Interactive prototypes and unsteered agent loops can assemble impressive demonstrations in an afternoon, yet falter when connected to multi-tenant databases, evolving policy documents, concurrent state transitions, and compliance audits. Closing that gap does not require abandoning the flexibility of language models. It requires surrounding the model with software engineering discipline: explicit task contracts, deterministic dispatchers, transactional write boundaries, provenance-preserving retrieval, durable state machines, and statistically honest evaluation.

The running example throughout the book is Northstar, a fictional software company whose customers export operational data. Northstar's support agent investigates why Account `A-17` under tenant `Cedar` experienced a nightly export failure (`X-58`, failing with `E_LIMIT_ROWS` at `18,432` rows) shortly after a subscription plan change from Pro to Standard. The investigation begins with four authorized read operations against ticket `T-104`, account `A-17`, export `X-58`, and the active Standard plan policy (`P-STD-2`, effective `2026-08-01` with a `10,000`-row limit, superseding the older `20,000`-row policy `P-STD-1`). From those first reads, the design develops into a cryptographically bound proposal and human approval workflow, an idempotent transactional commit, a checkpointed execution loop, a read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) stdio adapter, and an operational launch gate. The case is small enough to inspect on a single machine in Python's standard library and SQLite, yet rich enough to expose the failure modes that break much larger enterprise systems.

By the end of the book, you will be able to decide when a problem genuinely needs an agent rather than a deterministic rule or fixed workflow, write a one-page task contract before writing prompts, build a bounded model loop from scratch, design transactional tools that separate proposals from effects, ground claims in dated and scoped evidence, manage context and durable state, evaluate reliability across task families, defend against untrusted inputs, design human supervision that works under real review queues, coordinate specialists only when independent evidence justifies the overhead, and run a disciplined production launch.

## Who this book is for

This book is written for software engineers, AI engineers, and technical product builders comfortable with Python, HTTP APIs, relational databases, and typed schemas. You do not need prior experience with an agent framework. Chapters 1–4 deliberately implement the core runtime, dispatch table, and transactional store using only Python 3.11+ standard-library modules and SQLite so that every state transition, permission check, and failure mode remains visible. Later chapters show where frameworks, graph orchestrators, typed validation libraries, protocol adapters, and distributed serving infrastructure reduce boilerplate—and which safety responsibilities remain yours regardless of the library you adopt.

Engineering leaders, architects, and product managers can use the decision worksheets, task contracts, comparison tables, supervision rubrics, and release gates without typing every line of code. Security engineers and site reliability practitioners will find a concrete system on which to audit tenant isolation, least-privilege tool scopes, idempotency keys, lost-response reconciliation, and trace redaction. Domain experts and operations leads can use the acceptance criteria and scenario matrices to challenge systems that sound fluent in a demo but have not earned trust on boundary cases.

Appendix A explains how to run the local companion, execute its test suite, and inspect its action boundaries. Appendix B provides eight structured experiment protocols that you can execute against your own models and workloads. Appendix C defines the working engineering glossary. Each chapter concludes with hands-on exercises (with answer guidance) and routes into the 111-volume reference collection (109 distinct works) and primary technical specifications.

Work through the exercises using one real or realistic project of your own alongside Northstar. Keep your task contract, schema definitions, scenario fixtures, execution traces, and evaluation rubrics in version control. When a run fails or produces an unsupported claim, preserve the trace and classify the mechanism before editing a prompt. That engineering habit is far more valuable than stacking additional agent layers onto an unmeasured loop.

## Code, experiments, and evidence

A central discipline of this book is keeping different kinds of evidence distinct. In conversations about AI systems, it is easy for a fabricated illustration, a back-of-the-envelope cost formula, a deterministic unit test, and a live model benchmark to blur together. Throughout this book, every claim belongs to an explicit evidential category:

| Evidential category | What it establishes in this book | What it does not establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fictional domain fixtures (`Northstar`, `Cedar`, `Juniper`, `T-104`, `A-17`, `X-58`) | A controlled, inspectable problem space with known ground truth (`18,432` rows vs `10,000`-row `P-STD-2` limit and `20,000`-row `P-STD-1` history) | Empirical performance of any real company's support organization or production customer distribution |
| Offline component checks (`29 checks` in `test_northstar.py`, plus MCP and summary checks) | Deterministic verification of runtime boundaries: tenant scoping, schema rejection, digest integrity, version preconditions, expiry, idempotent replay, and restart | Live language-model reasoning quality, grounding accuracy on open-ended text, or resistance to novel adversarial attacks |
| Scripted model harness (`ScriptedModel`) | A deterministic test double that exercises the five-step read-and-propose loop and checkpoint recovery without network calls | Benchmark scores, latency distributions, or token efficiency of commercial or open-weight models |
| Mathematical and cost models | Explicit trade-off relationships (such as Value of Information, pass-all-`k` binomial reliability, and token-cost amplification across turns) under stated assumptions | Universal pricing or guaranteed production ROI without workload-specific telemetry |
| Literature synthesis and experiment protocols | Architectural patterns synthesized from 109 distinct technical works and eight reproducible evaluation protocols in Appendix B | Claimed measurements from unrun live trials or unexecuted human reviewer studies |

The companion contains the executable local support store and harness (`northstar.py`), the `29 checks` in `test_northstar.py`, the read-only MCP stdio server and client check, the trial-summary calculator, the 20 starter scenarios from Chapter 2 (`initial-scenarios.json`), and the full 200-scenario specification suite grouped into 40 families (`scenarios.jsonl`). No live model benchmark, human supervision study, practitioner interview, or production deployment is claimed as an executed result for Northstar. Where the text illustrates how to analyze trial tables or cost trade-offs, hypothetical numbers are explicitly labeled so that teaching arithmetic is never mistaken for empirical measurement.

## Using the companion

The electronic companion includes both the command-line Python package and an interactive browser explorer (`agent-explorer.html`). Itssix technical diagrams and two interactive calculators let you step through the bounded agent loop, compare layered state stores, inspect the proposal-approval-commit transaction, trace recovery paths after a lost response, and explore how per-run success rates and multi-turn token growth behave across repeated trials.

Every figure and table in the chapters is self-contained so you can read the book linearly without a computer in front of you. When you sit down to build, run `python3 test_northstar.py` first, inspect how each boundary failure is caught, and expand your agent's authority only as fast as your specifications, runtime guards, and verification checks can support it.


# 1. When Does a Problem Need an Agent?

## The request is small; the decision is not

At 09:12, a support ticket arrives at Northstar, a fictional software service that exports operational business data for enterprise tenants. A customer under tenant `Cedar` writes on ticket `T-104`: “Our nightly export failed after the plan change. Find the cause and prepare the support update.” On the surface, the sentence looks like a routine customer-service inquiry. Underneath, it leaves almost every operational constraint unspecified. It does not state which account or export job failed, which revision of the export policy governed the account at the time of execution, whether the subscription downgrade actually caused the error, or what mutations the support workflow is authorized to perform on live customer records.

An experienced support engineer resolves those ambiguities before touching a single setting. They verify that the requester belongs to tenant `Cedar`, read ticket `T-104` to identify account `A-17` and export job `X-58`, inspect the job telemetry (`18,432` rows, failing with error code `E_LIMIT_ROWS`), check the account's subscription history (recently downgraded from `Pro` to `Standard`), and look up the currently effective Standard policy (`P-STD-2`, effective `2026-08-01`, which caps exports at `10,000` rows, rather than the superseded policy `P-STD-1` that previously allowed `20,000` rows). Only after cross-checking those records do they draft an explanation and mark the ticket `INVESTIGATED`. Crucially, they also know what they are *not* allowed to do: they do not promise an unauthorized refund, silently upgrade `A-17` back to `Pro` (`100,000`-row limit under `P-PRO-1`), or re-run a heavy production export without explicit customer and operational approval.

That blend of targeted evidence gathering, policy interpretation, conditional branching, and strictly bounded authority makes the case an ideal proving ground for studying AI agents [[4]](#reference-4), [[52]](#reference-52). It also makes it an ideal place to practice resisting an agent when a simpler mechanism will do [[31]](#reference-31), [[97]](#reference-97). A software system that handles `T-104` might be a deterministic SQL query paired with a string template. It might be a search interface that surfaces records for a human analyst. It might be a single language-model call wrapped in application code, a multi-step workflow with fixed branches, or a bounded agent loop in which a model dynamically selects its next tool call based on intermediate observations [[26]](#reference-26), [[59]](#reference-59). In a five-minute stakeholder demo, all five architectures can be made to print the same paragraph on screen. Under production load, partial outages, stale documentation, or cross-tenant edge cases, they fail in radically different ways.

The foundational engineering question is therefore never “How do we make this system more agentic?” The right question is: *which specific decisions must be made dynamically at runtime from intermediate observations, what is the value of those observations, and what runtime boundaries justify delegating that control flow to a model?* [[57]](#reference-57), [[99]](#reference-99). Architecture follows from the structure of uncertainty and the cost of error. The label “agent” does not earn its complexity budget on its own.

This book follows Northstar from that initial support ticket to a verified production launch decision. Northstar, tenants `Cedar` and `Juniper`, and all associated tickets, accounts, exports, and policies are fabricated teaching fixtures. Because we control the exact state of the database and the exact rules of the domain, we can compare what the system *should* conclude against what it *actually* does at every step. That transparency is far more instructive than wrapping an opaque framework around an unverifiable task.

## Five ways to solve the same problem

When a team is asked to automate or accelerate a recurring task, the most productive first step is to lay out the full spectrum of candidate implementations, ordered by how much control flow remains fixed in application code versus delegated to a model [[26]](#reference-26), [[59]](#reference-59), [[97]](#reference-97). For Northstar's export investigation, five distinct designs are plausible.

The first design is a **deterministic rule or query**. Application code reads ticket `T-104`, joins the associated account `A-17` and export `X-58`, checks whether `error == "E_LIMIT_ROWS"` and `rows > limit_rows` under the active policy (`effective <= date('now')`), and renders a structured diagnostic record. When the error code is definitive and the schema captures all material variables, a deterministic rule is unbeatable: it executes in milliseconds, costs fractions of a cent, requires zero token budget, and cannot hallucinate a policy clause. Its primary engineering burden is maintaining rule coverage as error codes and schemas evolve.

The second design is a **search and context workspace** (assisted intelligence) [[99]](#reference-99). Whenever a support engineer opens `T-104`, the application retrieves the account history, the failed export metadata, and candidate policy documents (`P-STD-2`, `P-STD-1`, `P-PRO-1`), highlighting effective dates and row thresholds in a side panel. The human engineer performs the synthesis and writes the response. Search does not pretend to complete the investigation autonomously; its value is measured by reduced lookup latency and lower human citation error.

The third design is a **single language-model call** inside a fixed data pipeline. Deterministic application code fetches the authorized ticket, account, export, and current policy records, validates that they belong to tenant `Cedar`, and passes them in a single prompt to a language model to draft a customer-friendly explanation. Here, the model provides linguistic flexibility—translating structured database fields into clear prose—while application code retains 100% ownership of which records are fetched and which state transitions occur [[26]](#reference-26), [[52]](#reference-52).

The fourth design is an **orchestrated workflow** (or directed pipeline with model nodes) [[52]](#reference-52), [[97]](#reference-97). A classifier node categorizes the incoming ticket (`row_limit`, `timeout`, `permission_denied`, or `unknown`); a deterministic branch fetches the corresponding logs and policy documents; a drafting node generates a proposed response; and a validation gate checks required citations before queuing the draft for a human reviewer. Language models may be invoked two or three times along the path, and a router node may select among predefined branches, but the topology of the graph—which steps exist and what transitions are legal—is fixed in advance by the developer.

The fifth design is a **bounded agent**. Instead of hardcoding the sequence of reads, the runtime provides the model with a scoped set of tools (`read_ticket`, `read_account`, `read_export`, `read_policy`, `propose_update`) and a task goal [[4]](#reference-4), [[59]](#reference-59). After reading `T-104`, the model inspects the observation and chooses which tool to invoke next. If the ticket lacks an export ID, the model might query recent exports for the account or stop to ask the user for clarification. If the export failed with an unfamiliar error, it might inspect secondary diagnostic logs before selecting a policy document. Its next action is computed dynamically at runtime as a function of the accumulated observation history [[57]](#reference-57), [[97]](#reference-97).

| Design archetype | Who selects the next step? | Control-flow topology | Best suited when | Primary engineering and operational burden |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deterministic rule or query | Application code (`if`/`else`, SQL predicates) | Fixed, single-pass execution | Inputs are structured, error codes are definitive, and policy logic is exact | Keeping rules synchronized with schema and policy changes |
| Search assistant (Assisted AI) | Human operator | Human-driven lookup over indexed records | Evidence is scattered across repositories, but judgment carries high stakes | Retrieval precision, ranking freshness, and reviewer cognitive load |
| Single model call | Application code fetches data; model formats output | Fixed pre-fetch → one generation → post-check | Required evidence is known a priori, but output phrasing needs natural-language synthesis | Prompt grounding, output schema validation, and citation checks |
| Predefined workflow | Application graph (with optional model routing nodes) | Directed acyclic graph or fixed state machine with known branches | Task families follow repeatable standard operating procedures (SOPs) | Branch completeness, exception routing, and stage-to-stage error propagation |
| Bounded agent | Model selects actions within runtime-enforced guards | Dynamic loop (`observe → reason → act`) bounded by step/time budgets | Investigation paths vary dynamically based on intermediate observations | Loop termination, tool authorization, state checkpointing, and trajectory evaluation |

No row in this table is a universal upgrade over the rows above it [[31]](#reference-31), [[41]](#reference-41). Moving down the table trades structural predictability for runtime adaptability. In production engineering, simplicity does not mean writing a three-line framework call that hides a complex loop; simplicity means minimizing the number of independent ways a system can produce an unverified or unauthorized state change.

## Define agency through anatomy and control flow, not marketing labels

Because the term “AI agent” is used across the industry to describe everything from an autocomplete prompt to an autonomous cloud worker, architecture discussions quickly derail unless teams agree on concrete structural definitions [[52]](#reference-52), [[59]](#reference-59). In classical artificial intelligence, an agent is any entity that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon that environment through actuators to achieve an objective [[57]](#reference-57), [[59]](#reference-59). That broad definition applies equally to a thermostat, a reinforcement-learning policy controlling a robot arm, and an automated trading algorithm.

In modern software engineering with large language models, we use a more specific operational definition. As Grootendorst and Alammar illustrate in their anatomical breakdown of agent systems [[59]](#reference-59), an LLM-backed agent augments a core language model with modular capabilities that bridge text generation and environmental interaction:

1. **Perception and observations (sensors):** The mechanism by which the system ingests user requests, structured tool responses, database rows, document chunks, or multimodal inputs into its working context.
2. **Reasoning and planning (the model core):** An autoregressive or reasoning-trained language model that evaluates the current context, decomposes subgoals, weighs contradictions, and emits structured intent—either a final response or one or more tool-call proposals [[52]](#reference-52), [[59]](#reference-59).
3. **Memory and state management:** The separation between transient in-context history (the scratchpad or message array shipped on every turn) and durable external stores (checkpoints, authoritative business databases, and long-term knowledge indices) [[59]](#reference-59), [[97]](#reference-97).
4. **Action execution (actuators / tools):** Deterministic software interfaces that validate the model's proposed tool calls against schemas and permissions, execute authorized reads or writes against external services, and format the outcome as a new observation.

Crucially, the language model itself never executes a tool or mutates a database [[52]](#reference-52), [[59]](#reference-59). Fundamentally, an LLM is a stateless text-in, text-out (or token-in, token-out) function. When it emits `read_export(export_id="X-58")`, it has only generated a structured string expressing an *intention* to act. It is the **agent runtime**—the surrounding deterministic program—that parses that intention, verifies that the tool exists, checks that the caller holds the required authority, enforces step and latency budgets, executes the query, checkpoints the state, and decides whether the loop may continue [[4]](#reference-4), [[52]](#reference-52).

Koenigstein formalizes this runtime structure by modeling agents as **finite state machines (FSMs)** and **hierarchical state machines (HSMs)** [[52]](#reference-52). Even when a developer writes a simple `while` loop in Python, the system operates as a state machine governed by five explicit primitives:
- **State:** A compact, inspectable snapshot of what the runtime knows at a boundary (accumulated messages, step counters, token usage, and pending proposal IDs).
- **Event:** An occurrence that triggers a transition, such as the model returning a `tool_use` block, a tool raising a `BoundaryError`, or a wall-clock timer expiring.
- **Guard:** A deterministic predicate evaluated by the runtime before a transition is permitted—for example, checking `steps < max_steps`, verifying `principal.require("propose")`, or rejecting an unknown field in tool arguments.
- **Action:** The concrete work performed during a permitted transition, such as querying SQLite, persisting a run checkpoint, or recording a proposal digest.
- **Termination:** An explicit halting state (`answered`, `needs_approval`, `stopped`, or `failed`) that ends the loop and hands control back to the caller or human supervisor.

When systems grow to include planning, reflection, and human-in-the-loop review, flat state machines often suffer from edge explosion. Hierarchical state machines solve this by grouping substates (such as `PLAN`, `ACT`, and `REFLECT`) inside a parent superstate (`WORKING`) that enforces global guards—such as tenant isolation, token ceilings, and circuit breakers—once across all child transitions, while using shallow or deep history markers to resume cleanly after an interruption [[52]](#reference-52).

## Sequential decision-making and the Value of Information

Why delegate state transitions to a model at all if a deterministic state machine is so clean? Decision theory provides a rigorous answer [[57]](#reference-57). In *Algorithms for Decision Making*, Kochenderfer, Wheeler, and Wray distinguish between **open-loop plans**, where an entire sequence of actions is selected in advance before execution begins, and **closed-loop policies**, where the system selects each action `a_t = π(b_t)` based on its current *belief state* `b_t`—a summary of the initial request and all observations `o_1, …, o_t` gathered so far [[57]](#reference-57).

When the environment is **fully observable** and **deterministic**—for instance, every export ticket already arrives with a verified `account_id`, `export_id`, `error_code`, and `policy_id`—an open-loop pipeline is optimal. Fetching the four records in a fixed sequence yields the exact same information every time. Allowing a language model to decide the order of those four reads adds inference latency, token cost, and a non-zero probability of choosing a suboptimal action without improving the best achievable outcome.

An agent loop becomes mathematically and operationally justified when the problem is a **sequential decision process under partial observability** [[57]](#reference-57). In a partially observable environment, the true underlying state `s` (the actual root cause of the customer's failure) is hidden behind incomplete or noisy initial observations. Each diagnostic tool call is an information-gathering action that has a resource cost `c(a)` (latency, API fees, context window consumption, and downstream database load) and produces an observation `o` that updates the system's belief state.

In decision theory, the **Value of Information (VoI)** of an observation is the expected improvement in the quality of the final decision when the system conditions its action on that observation, minus the cost of acquiring it [[57]](#reference-57). Before calling a tool or adding an autonomous loop step, an engineer can ask three VoI questions:

1. **Can the observation change the terminal action?** If reading an auxiliary log file cannot change the diagnosis, the draft text, or the escalation decision under any plausible return value, its Value of Information is zero (or negative once token cost and context rot are included).
2. **Does the observation resolve ambiguity that blocks a safe decision?** In Northstar, reading `tickets` reveals `account_id="A-17"` and `export_id="X-58"`. Reading `accounts` reveals whether the customer is on `Standard` or `Pro`. Until `accounts` is observed, the system cannot know whether `P-STD-2` (`10,000` rows) or `P-PRO-1` (`100,000` rows) governs the export. The observation has high positive VoI because acting without it risks a severe policy misdiagnosis.
3. **Does the order of information gathering depend on what is found?** When a ticket says only “Our nightly integration broke after Tuesday's billing update,” the first observation might show `E_LIMIT_ROWS`, `E_AUTH_EXPIRED`, or zero failed exports under `A-17` (indicating the customer logged in from a secondary account). Here, the optimal second action depends on the outcome of the first action. Whenever the branching factor of diagnostic paths grows large enough that hardcoding every conditional tree becomes brittle or uneconomical, a closed-loop policy guided by a reasoning model begins to outperform a static pipeline [[57]](#reference-57), [[97]](#reference-97).

## The autonomy spectrum and human-AI division of labor

Even when a task benefits from closed-loop investigation, autonomy is not an all-or-nothing switch. Lipenkova frames AI product architecture along a continuum of **assisted**, **augmented**, and **autonomous** intelligence, emphasizing that successful products align the degree of delegation with the technical reliability of the model and the business cost of an error [[99]](#reference-99). Similarly, Koenigstein [[52]](#reference-52) and Grootendorst and Alammar [[59]](#reference-59) emphasize that production agency is multidimensional: a system can exercise high autonomy over read-only information foraging while operating under zero autonomy for external mutations.

Instead of asking whether Northstar's agent is “autonomous,” decompose autonomy across specific operational dimensions:

| Decision dimension | Level 0: Deterministic / Assisted | Level 1: Fixed Workflow / Augmented | Level 2: Bounded Agent (Northstar Ch. 3–4 target) | Level 3: High-Autonomy Agent (Requires Ch. 8–16 gates) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Information gathering (Reads)** | Fixed SQL query or human manual search | Predefined multi-step fetch by ticket category | Model dynamically selects authorized read tools within `max_steps` | Model formulates multi-hop queries across federated MCP sources |
| **Hypothesis & interpretation** | Exact boolean predicate (`rows > limit_rows`) | Model summarizes pre-fetched records into a template | Model cross-checks observations, resolves date/version conflicts, or abstains | Model plans multi-stage diagnostic hypotheses and self-critiques |
| **Internal state mutation (Proposals)** | None (read-only view) | Automatically attaches draft note to internal queue | Model calls `propose_update` to create an immutable, hashed proposal | Model updates low-risk internal triage tags automatically |
| **External or authoritative writes** | Human edits database directly | Human copies draft and clicks Update | **Human reviewer approves digest**; deterministic service executes `commit` | Conditional auto-commit only on verified low-risk families with rollback |
| **Scope & boundary expansion** | Fixed in code | Fixed in workflow definition | Strictly forbidden (`unknown_tool_or_invalid_fields` fails closed) | Escalates to human supervisor to request temporary scope elevation |

Notice where Northstar's initial architecture sits in this matrix. In Chapters 3 and 4, we grant the agent **Level 2 autonomy over read-only investigation and proposal drafting**, while holding **authoritative ticket updates at a strict human approval gate** and keeping **external side effects (sending customer emails, altering billing plans, issuing refunds, or retrying exports) completely outside the tool vocabulary** [[52]](#reference-52), [[99]](#reference-99).

This asymmetric allocation of autonomy is one of the most important patterns in production AI engineering. Investigation is read-only and reversible; its worst-case failure mode is wasted tokens or a flawed draft that a reviewer rejects. Remediation mutates authoritative business state or communicates with customers; its failure modes include financial loss, cross-tenant data leakage, and broken audit trails. By decoupling investigation autonomy from mutation authority, teams can capture 80% of the productivity gain of an agent while containing the blast radius of model errors [[97]](#reference-97), [[99]](#reference-99).

## The Northstar case, made explicit

Let us state the exact data invariants of the Northstar running example so that every architectural claim in Chapters 1–16 can be checked against concrete records.

Northstar serves multiple enterprise tenants, including `Cedar` and `Juniper`. Every business table in Northstar's relational store (`tickets`, `accounts`, `exports`, `policies`, and `commits`) is partitioned by a `tenant` column. Under tenant `Cedar`:
- **Ticket `T-104`** references `account_id="A-17"` and `export_id="X-58"`. Its initial `status` is `"OPEN"`, its `draft_reply` is empty (`""`), and its optimistic concurrency `version` is `1`.
- **Account `A-17`** has current `plan="Standard"` and `previous_plan="Pro"`.
- **Export `X-58`** recorded `rows=18432` and failed with `error="E_LIMIT_ROWS"`.
- **Policy table (`policies`)** contains three records for each tenant:
  1. `plan="Standard"`, `limit_rows=10000`, `effective="2026-08-01"`, `doc_id="P-STD-2"` (the active Standard policy).
  2. `plan="Standard"`, `limit_rows=20000`, `effective="2026-01-01"`, `doc_id="P-STD-1"` (the superseded Standard policy).
  3. `plan="Pro"`, `limit_rows=100000`, `effective="2026-08-01"`, `doc_id="P-PRO-1"` (the active Pro policy).

To prevent cross-tenant accidents from looking like simple missing-record bugs during testing, the local fixture seeds identical identifiers (`T-104`, `A-17`, `X-58`) under tenant `Juniper` as well. If a poorly designed tool looks up `WHERE id = 'T-104'` without binding `tenant = principal.tenant` from trusted server state, it risks reading or mutating `Juniper`'s data during a `Cedar` investigation.

Why is this tiny dataset so effective at exposing architectural flaws? Because it embeds five classic production traps in a single screen of data:
1. **Temporal policy confusion:** A naive vector search over policy documentation for “Standard plan row limit” will retrieve both `P-STD-1` (`20,000` rows) and `P-STD-2` (`10,000` rows). If the agent selects `P-STD-1`, it will falsely conclude that `18,432` rows is *below* the `20,000`-row limit and hallucinate an unrelated infrastructure bug.
2. **Unverified customer premise:** If the customer writes “We are on Pro and our export failed,” an ungrounded model may take the customer's word for the plan tier, apply `P-PRO-1` (`100,000` rows), and miss the fact that `A-17` was downgraded to `Standard`.
3. **Cross-tenant confusion:** If the model is allowed to pass `tenant` as a tool argument, a prompt injection or hallucination can pivot the investigation from `Cedar` to `Juniper`.
4. **Conflating intent with effect:** A model that outputs “I have updated ticket T-104 and notified the customer” has only emitted tokens. Unless a proposal was approved and committed in a verified database transaction, the ticket in SQLite is still `OPEN` at `version=1`.
5. **Scope creep into remediation:** A helpful-sounding model might promise “I have temporarily raised your Standard limit to 20,000 rows and queued a retry of X-58,” inventing capabilities the system does not possess and creating an immediate customer-trust incident.

## A production failure taxonomy for agent systems

Before writing a line of agent code, engineers should understand how loop-based systems fail in production. Drawing on Koenigstein's threat and failure analyses [[52]](#reference-52), Valenx Press's loop anti-patterns [[97]](#reference-97), and Lipenkova's product risk framework [[99]](#reference-99), we can classify agent failures into six structural categories:

| Failure category | Mechanism in an unguarded agent | Concrete Northstar manifestation | Architectural countermeasure (Chapters 1–7) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Runaway or non-terminating loop** | Success condition (“inbox empty” or “cause found”) is treated as a termination condition; tool errors trigger infinite self-correction retries [[97]](#reference-97) | Agent repeatedly calls `read_policy` with guessed plan names (`"Enterprise"`, `"Basic"`) until context overflows | Separate success from termination; enforce hard `max_steps`, `max_seconds`, and `max_total_tokens` guards (Ch. 3) |
| **Temporal or provenance drift** | Retrieval ranks chunks by lexical similarity without enforcing effective-date intervals or source authority | Agent cites superseded policy `P-STD-1` (`20,000` rows) instead of active `P-STD-2` (`10,000` rows) | Enforce temporal predicates (`effective <= date('now')`) and preserve structured provenance metadata (Ch. 2, Ch. 5) |
| **Confused deputy / tenant breach** | Identity or tenant scope is passed in prompts or model-supplied tool parameters rather than bound to authenticated server context | Model passes `tenant="Juniper"` or follows an injected instruction inside ticket text to read another customer's account | Bind immutable `Principal` in trusted code; reject extra tool fields (`additionalProperties: False`) (Ch. 3, Ch. 4) |
| **Phantom or unverified side effect** | Application treats the model's natural-language completion as proof that a state change occurred | Model replies “Ticket T-104 is now INVESTIGATED,” while `propose_update` failed validation and the database remains `OPEN` | Separate `answered` from `needs_approval` and verified `commit` receipts; verify postconditions in SQL (Ch. 3, Ch. 4) |
| **Duplicate mutation on retry** | Network timeout or worker crash after commit causes the loop or caller to re-issue a non-idempotent write [[97]](#reference-97) | A retried commit increments ticket version twice or overwrites a concurrent edit; in financial tools, issues duplicate refunds | Require an `idem_key` stored atomically with the committed receipt inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (Ch. 4, Ch. 7) |
| **Stale-evidence execution (TOCTOU)** | State changes between the time the agent inspects records (or a human approves a proposal) and the time the write executes | Reviewer approves a Standard-limit draft for `T-104`, but `A-17` upgrades back to `Pro` before commit | Hash material evidence into the proposal `digest` and recheck both `expected_version` and `evidence` inside the commit transaction (Ch. 4) |

Notice a striking pattern across this table: *none of these six production failure modes can be solved reliably by editing the system prompt alone.* Telling a model “Do not loop forever,” “Only read Cedar records,” or “Do not duplicate writes on timeout” asks a probabilistic token generator to enforce systems-level invariants it cannot even observe. Reliable agent engineering places probabilistic reasoning inside deterministic harnesses [[51]](#reference-51), [[52]](#reference-52), [[97]](#reference-97).

## Look for decision variability, not conversational polish

A natural-language chat box can make a rigid three-step script feel remarkably lifelike. Conversely, a background worker triggered by a database webhook with zero chat interface can be a genuine multi-step agent. Never confuse the user interface with the control-flow architecture [[26]](#reference-26), [[99]](#reference-99).

To decide whether a task warrants dynamic model-directed control flow, evaluate three structural properties of the workload:

First, **input and path variability**. Can the engineering team write down a flowchart in which all branches and required data fetches are known before execution starts? As *The 0→1 Loop Engineering Playbook* observes, if you can draw a complete flowchart with all branches known in advance, build a pipeline; if the branches depend on what the system discovers at runtime, consider a loop [[97]](#reference-97). For standard `E_LIMIT_ROWS` failures where the ticket always links a valid `account_id` and `export_id`, the four-read pipeline (`baseline`) is sufficient. When tickets arrive with missing export identifiers, ambiguous timestamps around a plan transition, or composite failures across multiple jobs, dynamic tool selection allows the investigator to adapt its path to what the first read reveals.

Second, **environmental observability**. Does the tool surface actually expose the evidence needed to resolve the ambiguity? An agent cannot compensate for a missing audit log by generating more reasoning tokens [[59]](#reference-59). If Northstar's database does not record when `A-17` switched from `Pro` to `Standard`, no amount of chain-of-thought prompting can establish whether the export ran before or after the downgrade. In that situation, the only reliable behavior is to identify the missing evidence and abstain or escalate.

Third, **verifiability of the terminal state**. Can an automated check or a human reviewer verify the output in less time than it would take to do the task from scratch [[31]](#reference-31), [[99]](#reference-99)? In Northstar, a reviewer can inspect a structured preview showing `18,432` rows, `E_LIMIT_ROWS`, `Standard` plan, and `P-STD-2` (`10,000` rows) in seconds. If verifying an agent's output requires re-running the entire investigation manually because provenance is not captured, the agent has not reduced operational work—it has merely shifted the work from authoring to forensic auditing.

## A pre-architecture decision worksheet

Before selecting an orchestration library or provisioning model endpoints, walk through the following engineering worksheet with both a domain practitioner and the engineer who will own on-call operations [[41]](#reference-41), [[99]](#reference-99).

| Worksheet question | Concrete evidence to collect | Northstar interpretation | Architectural consequence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Does the task family recur at volume?** | Historical ticket distribution by category and resolution time | Export failures are a top-tier recurring support category; rare billing disputes are not | Automate routine export triage; route rare contractual disputes directly to humans |
| **2. Is the information-gathering path predictable?** | Trace 50 real historical resolutions step by step | Clear `E_LIMIT_ROWS` tickets follow a 4-read path; incomplete tickets require adaptive lookups | Implement the 4-read `baseline` first; use the bounded agent loop only where paths branch dynamically |
| **3. Are authoritative sources accessible and dated?** | Schema inspection, API latency, policy versioning audit | `tickets`, `accounts`, `exports`, and effective-dated `policies` (`P-STD-2` vs `P-STD-1`) are queryable | Enforce `effective <= date('now')` in `read_policy`; attach structured evidence snapshots to every proposal |
| **4. What is the total cost of an error?** | Blast radius of wrong reads vs wrong writes [[99]](#reference-99) | A wrong draft wastes reviewer time; an unauthorized plan change or cross-tenant leak is severe | Allow autonomous reads (`read` scope); gate ticket updates behind human `approve` + transactional `commit` |
| **5. Can success and failure be checked deterministically?** | Acceptance predicates, database postconditions, citation rules | Status (`OPEN` → `INVESTIGATED`), version (`1` → `2`), and cited policy (`P-STD-2`) are exact | Encode 20 starter scenarios (Ch. 2) and 29 deterministic boundary checks (`test_northstar.py`) |
| **6. Who absorbs unresolved or escalated work?** | Staffing capacity, queue SLAs, reviewer permissions | Support reviewers hold `approve` and `commit` scopes for tenant `Cedar` | Ensure stopped or escalated runs attach partial observations so reviewers never start from zero |
| **7. What is the non-agent baseline?** | Existing deterministic rule, SQL script, or fixed workflow | `baseline(store, principal, ticket_id)` in `northstar.py` | Benchmark any live model loop against `baseline` on both routine and ambiguous scenario families |

Treat this worksheet as a set of falsifiable gates rather than a numerical scorecard. A project that scores high on ticket volume and executive enthusiasm but lacks dated policy records or a human escalation queue will fail in production. Each row tells you what infrastructure you must build *before* you turn on an agent loop.

## Total cost of ownership and the economics of error

Teams frequently estimate the cost of an agent by multiplying expected prompt tokens by the provider's per-million-token price. That calculation captures only the visible tip of the operational invoice [[97]](#reference-97), [[99]](#reference-99).

First, **loop steps multiply token consumption rather than adding to it linearly** [[97]](#reference-97). Because language models are stateless across calls, every turn in an agent loop re-sends the system prompt, the tool schemas, the user request, and every prior assistant tool call and tool observation accumulated so far. If turn 1 sends `1{,}500` input tokens and receives a `500`-token observation, turn 2 sends `2{,}000` input tokens, turn 3 sends `2{,}600`, and by turn 8 the cumulative input tokens billed across the run can be five to six times the size of the final context window. When an unguarded loop gets stuck retrying a failing tool up to `MAX_STEPS = 20` across thousands of concurrent requests, token spend compounds rapidly [[97]](#reference-97).

Second, **the cost of human review and error remediation often dwarfs inference spend** [[99]](#reference-99). Lipenkova emphasizes evaluating AI products through the interaction of task frequency, automation rate, and the *cost of error recovery* [[99]](#reference-99). Suppose an automated workflow drafts 100 support responses for \$2.00 in model fees. If 15 of those drafts cite the superseded `20,000`-row limit (`P-STD-1`) or promise an unauthorized export retry, and a senior support engineer must spend 12 minutes per flawed ticket untangling the confusion, auditing logs, and writing a corrective follow-up, those 15 errors consume three hours of specialized engineering labor—plus customer goodwill. Saving thirty seconds of typing on 85 easy tickets does not pay for fifteen subtle policy fabrications.

We can express the net operational value of an agentic workflow per task using an explicit engineering accounting model (adapted from product and decision-theoretic analysis [[57]](#reference-57), [[99]](#reference-99)):

```
Net Value per Task = p_auto · (C_manual - C_review_ok) - p_esc · C_handoff - p_err · C_remediate - C_compute
```

where:
- `p_auto`, `p_esc`, and `p_err` are the proportions of tasks that result in a verified correct proposal, a clean escalation/stop, and an undetected or flawed output requiring rework (`p_auto + p_esc + p_err = 1`).
- `C_manual` is the baseline cost (in engineer time and compute) of resolving the ticket without the agent.
- `C_review_ok` is the human supervision cost of inspecting and approving a valid proposal preview.
- `C_handoff` is the friction added when an agent stops mid-investigation and hands off to a human (which is low when the trace is clean and structured, and high when the human must decipher a rambling chat log).
- `C_remediate` is the full business and operational cost of a flawed output or bad mutation.
- `C_compute` is the expected inference, tool-call, storage, and observability cost across all turns of the loop.

Notice two immediate engineering insights from this equation. First, if `C_remediate` is large (for example, an unguarded tool issues duplicate financial refunds [[97]](#reference-97) or leaks `Juniper` records to `Cedar`), even a tiny error rate `p_err = 0.01` makes the entire system net-negative. Moving consequential writes behind a deterministic validation and approval gate drives `C_remediate` down by catching bad proposals before they become external effects. Second, making escalations clean and structured reduces `C_handoff`: an agent that recognizes missing evidence on step 2 and attaches the verified `ticket` and `account` records still saves the human reviewer lookup time even when it cannot finish the diagnosis.

*(Note: The companion's interactive cost calculator uses explicitly hypothetical unit costs to let you explore these sensitivity curves; it does not report empirical benchmark numbers for Northstar.)*

Latency follows the same multi-part structure. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) measures how quickly a chat UI begins streaming characters, not how quickly a business problem is solved. In a five-step investigation that executes four database reads, creates a proposal, and waits in a human approval queue before committing, end-to-end resolution time is the sum of sequential model turns, tool execution latencies, and review queue wait time. Streaming “Looking into your export…” in 300 milliseconds does not make a 45-second loop fast. Always track **time to verified terminal state** separately from model response latency.

## What a credible baseline protects you from

One of the most common mistakes in applied AI teams is comparing a newly built, heavily prompted agent using a frontier reasoning model against a strawman baseline—or against no baseline at all [[31]](#reference-31), [[41]](#reference-41). A credible baseline is the simplest non-agentic (or lower-autonomy) implementation given access to the exact same authorized data sources and evaluated against the exact same acceptance criteria.

In the companion (`northstar.py`), the `baseline` function is twelve lines of readable Python:

```python
def baseline(store, principal, ticket_id="T-104"):
    """Fixed control flow for the known export-limit task; does not use a model."""
    ticket = store.read(principal, "read_ticket", ticket_id)
    account = store.read(principal, "read_account", ticket["account_id"])
    export = store.read(principal, "read_export", ticket["export_id"])
    policy = store.read(principal, "read_policy", account["plan"])
    supported = export["error"] == "E_LIMIT_ROWS" and export["rows"] > policy["limit_rows"]
    return {
        "state": "supported" if supported else "needs_investigation",
        "ticket_id": ticket["id"], "account_id": account["id"],
        "plan": account["plan"], "rows": export["rows"],
        "limit_rows": policy["limit_rows"], "policy": policy["doc_id"],
        "model_calls": 0,
    }
```

Look closely at what `baseline` achieves on the canonical `T-104` case:
1. It enforces tenant isolation and `read` scope by calling `store.read(principal, ...)`—the exact same data-access method the agent's tools use.
2. It retrieves the active policy (`P-STD-2`, `10,000` rows) using the same effective-date query (`effective <= date('now') ORDER BY effective DESC LIMIT 1`).
3. It checks the exact business predicate (`export["error"] == "E_LIMIT_ROWS" and export["rows"] > policy["limit_rows"]`) and returns `state="supported"` with `policy="P-STD-2"` and `model_calls=0`.
4. When the predicate does not hold—for instance, if `rows` is `9,999` or the error is an unfamiliar timeout—it does not guess; it cleanly returns `state="needs_investigation"`.

Maintaining this baseline alongside your agent protects your engineering judgment in three ways:
- **It forces task-family stratification.** On ordinary `E_LIMIT_ROWS` tickets where all foreign keys are present, `baseline` achieves 100% accuracy with zero token cost and sub-millisecond latency. An agent cannot beat `baseline` on that slice; it can only tie it at higher cost. The agent's value must be proved on *other* scenario families: tickets where the identifier is embedded in unstructured prose, where multiple exports exist for the same account, or where natural-language synthesis of a nuanced draft saves measurable reviewer time.
- **It inspires hybrid routing architectures.** Once you see that `baseline` handles standard row-limit mismatches deterministically, the right production architecture is rarely “replace `baseline` with an agent.” Instead, run the deterministic check first (or route known error codes to `baseline`), and invoke the bounded agent loop only when `baseline` returns `needs_investigation` [[97]](#reference-97), [[99]](#reference-99).
- **It isolates control-flow value from model-upgrade effects.** When a team upgrades from a small model to a frontier reasoning model at the same time they switch from a fixed workflow to an autonomous loop, they conflate two independent variables. Testing the same model inside a fixed workflow versus inside a dynamic loop tells you whether dynamic action selection is actually helping.

## Build a boundary before building ambition

Every chapter in this book follows a deliberate progression: **define the boundary first, verify that the boundary holds under faults, and only then widen the capability** [[11]](#reference-11), [[52]](#reference-52).

For Northstar, that progression unfolds in clear stages:
1. **Stage 1 (Chapters 1–2): Problem selection and contract specification.** Define what the investigator is allowed to read, what it may propose, what effects are strictly excluded, and which 20 starter scenarios test those boundaries.
2. **Stage 2 (Chapter 3): Read-and-propose loop with explicit dispatch.** Give the model read tools (`read_ticket`, `read_account`, `read_export`, `read_policy`) and a single proposal tool (`propose_update`) that writes an immutable record to `proposals` without touching `tickets`. Enforce strict schema validation, tenant scoping, step caps (`max_steps=8`), wall-clock deadlines (`max_seconds=60`), and checkpoint persistence (`runs`).
3. **Stage 3 (Chapter 4): Human approval and transactional commit.** Require a reviewer holding `approve` and `commit` scopes to inspect the proposal digest, record an approval, and execute an atomic SQLite transaction (`BEGIN IMMEDIATE`) that re-verifies ticket version, status, proposal expiry, digest integrity, and material evidence (`account`, `export`, `policy`) before updating `tickets` from `OPEN` to `INVESTIGATED` at `version=2` and storing an idempotent commit receipt.
4. **Stage 4 (Chapters 5–7): Grounded retrieval, layered state, and crash recovery.** Expand the evidence model to handle multi-document retrieval with temporal validity, manage context growth without erasing provenance, and reconcile interrupted or timed-out operations.
5. **Stage 5 (Chapters 8–16): Evaluation, security, supervision, protocols, and launch.** Scale verification across 200 scenarios in 40 families, harden against indirect prompt injection, design review queues that prevent rubber-stamping, expose read capabilities over MCP, control token economics, and run a formal pre-launch gate.

Resist the temptation to jump straight to multi-agent swarms or autonomous write loops in week one. When an unguarded prototype fails, you cannot tell whether the prompt was vague, the tool schema was ambiguous, the retrieval returned a stale document, or the database state changed mid-run. Building the boundaries stage by stage ensures that every failure has an identifiable address.

## Worked architectural review: rejecting premature multi-agent complexity

Suppose a well-meaning engineering team proposes building Northstar's ticket investigator as a five-agent collaborative mesh:
1. A **Triage Planner Agent** that decomposes the ticket into subtasks.
2. A **Database Researcher Agent** that queries `tickets`, `accounts`, and `exports`.
3. A **Policy Legal Analyst Agent** that searches policy documents and debates edge cases with the Researcher.
4. A **Customer Communications Writer Agent** that drafts empathetic prose.
5. A **Supervisor Critic Agent** that grades the draft and routes revisions back to the Writer.

In a slide deck, this architecture looks thorough and sophisticated. Before writing a single class, subject the proposal to a first-principles engineering review [[31]](#reference-31), [[52]](#reference-52), [[97]](#reference-97):

**Question 1: What independent information source or distinct permission boundary does each agent hold?**
In the proposed five-agent design, all five agents operate within the same tenant (`Cedar`), inspect the same four small records (`T-104`, `A-17`, `X-58`, `P-STD-2`), and call the same underlying language model endpoint. The Policy Analyst has no special legal database that the Researcher lacks; it only has a different system prompt (“You are a meticulous policy analyst”). Passing natural-language summaries across five conversational handoffs does not create new evidence—it introduces four serialization boundaries where exact numbers (`18,432` vs `10,000`) and policy identifiers (`P-STD-2` vs `P-STD-1`) can be paraphrased, softened, or dropped.

**Question 2: What happens to latency, token cost, and failure surfaces?**
A single bounded investigator completes the canonical Northstar path in five deterministic tool steps. A five-agent conversational mesh with a critic loop easily turns five steps into fifteen or twenty model invocations, multiplying input-token billing and pushing latency from seconds to minutes. Worse, if the Critic Agent repeatedly demands stylistic edits while the Writer Agent drops the policy citation to satisfy tone feedback, the multi-agent loop can oscillate until its budget expires [[97]](#reference-97).

**Question 3: When *would* a second agent or isolated sub-workflow be justified?**
A separate agent or sub-machine earns its keep when it enforces a **genuine boundary of context, privilege, or modality** [[52]](#reference-52), [[59]](#reference-59). For example, if Northstar later adds an automated log-parsing specialist that ingests 50 megabytes of raw stack traces in a sandboxed container and returns a 200-token structured summary, isolating that noisy diagnostic context in a sub-agent prevents raw log dumps from polluting the main investigator's context window. Similarly, separating the untrusted investigation loop (`INVESTIGATOR` principal with `read` and `propose` scopes) from the privileged commit path (`REVIEWER` principal with `approve` and `commit` scopes) is essential—and in Chapter 4 we enforce that separation directly in the runtime and database rather than trusting two prompts to police each other.

Write competing architectures on a single page. List the exact inputs, state transitions, permission scopes, worst-case token budgets, and failure modes of each. If a simpler single-loop or hybrid baseline-plus-agent design satisfies the task contract with fewer moving parts, choose the simpler design and spend the saved engineering time on evaluation scenarios and transactional tool safety.

## Exercises and answer guidance

**Exercise 1: Reject an unnecessary agent.**
A product team proposes building an autonomous LLM agent to validate incoming CSV export configurations (checking that `delimiter` is a single ASCII character, `max_rows` is an integer between `1` and `100,000`, `date_format` is ISO-8601, and the requested `columns` exist in the tenant's table schema). Explain why an agent loop is the wrong architecture here, and specify the right design.
*Answer guidance:* All rules and inputs are fully observable, structured, and deterministic. Delegating schema validation to an LLM introduces probabilistic false positives/negatives, 100× higher latency, and unnecessary token spend [[31]](#reference-31), [[97]](#reference-97). The right design is a deterministic validator (such as a Pydantic model or JSON Schema validator paired with a schema catalog lookup) that returns exact field-level error codes. Reserve a language model, if needed at all, for an optional assistive step that translates a user's natural-language export request into a candidate JSON configuration *before* the deterministic validator checks it.

**Exercise 2: Distinguish interface from control flow.**
Sketch two system designs for Northstar support: (a) a conversational chat UI backed by a fixed workflow (`baseline`), and (b) a structured web form (“Click to Investigate Ticket”) backed by a bounded five-step agent loop (`run_agent`). For each design, state who selects the next action at runtime and what failure modes dominate.
*Answer guidance:* In (a), the user types natural language, an intent extractor pulls out `T-104`, and deterministic application code executes the exact four-read sequence; the model never chooses which tool to call next. Its main failure mode is entity extraction failure on conversational input. In (b), the user clicks a button with no chat prompt, and the agent loop dynamically selects tool calls over five turns to produce a proposal. Its main failure modes are loop non-termination, wrong tool selection, or misinterpreting intermediate observations [[26]](#reference-26), [[59]](#reference-59). Interface modality (`chat` vs `button`) is orthogonal to control-flow delegation (`workflow` vs `agent`).

**Exercise 3: Compute Value of Information (VoI) for a candidate tool call.**
Suppose an investigator examining `T-104` has already read the ticket (`A-17`, `X-58`), the export (`18,432` rows, `E_LIMIT_ROWS`), and the account (`plan="Standard"`, `previous_plan="Pro"`). Consider two candidate next tool calls: (a) `read_policy(plan="Standard")`, and (b) a hypothetical `read_ui_theme_preferences(account_id="A-17")` tool. Analyze both using Value of Information [[57]](#reference-57).
*Answer guidance:* Call (a) has high positive VoI: before reading the policy, the agent cannot distinguish whether the active Standard limit is `20,000` rows (`P-STD-1`, under which `18,432` rows should have succeeded and `E_LIMIT_ROWS` indicates a bug) or `10,000` rows (`P-STD-2`, under which `18,432` rows legitimately violates the plan limit). The observation directly determines the diagnosis and draft. Call (b) has negative net VoI: UI theme preferences cannot alter export row limits or error codes under any return value, so calling it pays latency and token costs while adding distractor tokens to the context window.

**Exercise 4: Map the Northstar loop to Finite State Machine (FSM) primitives.**
Using Koenigstein's five FSM primitives (State, Event, Guard, Action, Termination) [[52]](#reference-52), write out the exact state transition that occurs when the Northstar agent invokes `propose_update` on step 5 of its investigation of `T-104`.
*Answer guidance:* **State:** `runs` record with `steps=4`, `state="stopped"` (in-progress), and `messages` containing four validated `tool_result` observations (`T-104`, `A-17`, `X-58`, `P-STD-2`). **Event:** Model returns an assistant message containing a `tool_use` block for `propose_update(ticket_id="T-104", expected_version=1, draft_reply=...)`. **Guards:** Runtime verifies `steps < max_steps`, `time.monotonic() < deadline`, `len(calls) <= 5`, `name in TOOL_FIELDS`, exact argument keys, `type(expected_version) is int`, `20 <= len(draft_reply) <= 2000`, `principal.require("propose")`, `ticket["version"] == 1`, and `ticket["status"] == "OPEN"`. **Action:** Compute SHA-256 `digest` over `[tenant, ticket_id, expected_version, changes, evidence]`, insert immutable row into `proposals` with 900-second expiry, append `tool_result` to `messages`, and checkpoint the run to SQLite. **Termination:** Because the observation returns `state == "needs_approval"`, the loop transitions to terminal runtime state `needs_approval` and breaks without mutating `tickets`.

**Exercise 5: Evaluate operational net value under error costs.**
Using the net operational value formula from this chapter, suppose a support team processes 1,000 export tickets per week. Manual investigation costs $12.00 per ticket in engineer time (`C_manual = 12`). A proposed agent costs $0.15 per run in compute (`C_compute = 0.15`). Reviewing and approving a correct proposal costs $2.00 (`C_review_ok = 2`). Handling a clean escalation costs $12.50 (`C_handoff = 12.50`). However, if an unreviewed agent auto-sends a flawed response or bad account mutation, remediating the customer incident costs $180.00 (`C_remediate = 180`). Compare Configuration A (auto-send without review: `p_auto = 0.85` with `C_review_ok = 0, p_esc = 0.05, p_err = 0.10`) against Configuration B (proposal + human approval gate that catches 95% of errors during review: `p_auto = 0.85` with `C_review_ok = 2, p_esc = 0.145, p_err = 0.005`).
*Answer guidance:* Under Configuration A (auto-send), per-task savings on the 85% correct runs are `0.85 × 12 = $10.20`, minus escalation cost `0.05 × 12.50 = $0.625`, minus remediation cost `0.10 × 180 = $18.00`, minus compute `$0.15`, yielding **-$8.575 per ticket** (or a total cost of `0.05 × 12.50 + 0.10 × 180 + 0.15 = $18.775` per ticket vs. $12.00 manual, losing $6.78 per ticket). Under Configuration B (gated review), net value over manual is `0.85 × (12 - 2) - 0.145 × (12.50 - 12) - 0.005 × 180 - 0.15 = 8.50 - 0.0725 - 0.90 - 0.15 = +$7.38` per ticket saved over manual resolution. The human approval gate turns a value-destroying autonomous deployment into a net-positive engineering system [[99]](#reference-99).

**Exercise 6: Design a hybrid routing baseline.**
Specify a two-stage architecture for Northstar that combines `baseline` with `run_agent`. State the exact entry condition for Stage 1, the handoff condition to Stage 2, and how you would evaluate whether Stage 2 earns its incremental cost.
*Answer guidance:* Stage 1 runs `baseline(store, principal, ticket_id)` whenever a ticket arrives with a non-empty `ticket_id`. If `baseline` returns `state == "supported"`, a deterministic template formats the `P-STD-2` draft and submits it directly to `store.propose` with zero model calls. If `baseline` returns `state == "needs_investigation"` (or raises `not_found_or_not_authorized` because the user supplied free-text symptoms rather than a structured `export_id`), the router invokes Stage 2 (`run_agent`), passing the already-fetched `ticket`, `account`, and `export` observations in the initial context so the agent does not pay tokens to re-read them. Evaluate Stage 2 solely on the `needs_investigation` cohort, measuring verified proposal accuracy and reviewer time saved per dollar of token spend.

## Further reading

Lanham's *AI Agents in Action, Second Edition* [[4]](#reference-4) and Grootendorst and Alammar's *An Illustrated Guide to AI Agents* [[59]](#reference-59) provide clear component-level introductions to perception, reasoning models, memory, planning, and tool execution. Koenigstein's *AI Agents: The Definitive Guide* [[52]](#reference-52) develops the foundational blueprint from standalone LLMs to finite and hierarchical state machines (FSMs/HSMs), bounded autonomy, and production threat and failure taxonomies.

Kochenderfer, Wheeler, and Wray's *Algorithms for Decision Making* [[57]](#reference-57) establishes the mathematical foundations of sequential decision problems under uncertainty, open-loop versus closed-loop policies, partially observable state (POMDPs), and the Value of Information (VoI). Valenx Press's *The 0→1 Loop Engineering Playbook, 2026 Edition* [[97]](#reference-97) contrasts deterministic pipelines with autonomous loop archetypes, highlighting multiplicative step costs, runaway-loop incidents, and the distinction between success conditions and termination conditions.

De Mauro's *Grokking AI Applications* [[26]](#reference-26) traces the engineering progression from direct model calls to tool-enabled workflows. Bhavsar's *Mastering AI Agents* [[31]](#reference-31) examines evaluation criteria and cases where agent complexity is unwarranted. Lipenkova's *The Art of AI Product Development* [[99]](#reference-99) and Nika and Granados's *The AI Product Playbook* [[41]](#reference-41) connect technical capability, assisted/augmented/autonomous intelligence modes, and the total cost of error to disciplined product selection. Anthropic's engineering note [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) complements these works with a concise practitioner taxonomy of workflows versus agents.


# 2. Specify the Job Before Building the Agent

## Why unstructured prompting fails in enterprise systems

“Handle this support ticket” works when spoken to a seasoned colleague because human engineers carry an unspoken mental contract into every task. A support engineer at Northstar already knows which tenant's database rows they are permitted to inspect, how to tell an active policy apart from an archived draft, which promises would bind the company to a billing credit, and when an ambiguous customer request belongs to the account-management team rather than technical support. An AI agent inherits none of that institutional judgment from a system prompt that says, “You are a helpful, expert customer support agent.”

Across software organizations, teams have learned the hard way what happens when they skip explicit task specification and rely instead on informal, iterative prompting—a workflow popularized as “vibe coding” or vibe-driven agent development [[74]](#reference-74). As Alto documents in *Enterprise Vibe Coding for Agentic Engineering* [[74]](#reference-74), unstructured prompting feels magical during a weekend prototype: a developer describes a high-level outcome, the model generates plausible tool calls or application code, and early velocity spikes. Yet when that same workflow meets enterprise production—where multiple teams review changes, compliance rules govern tenant data, and systems must be maintained by engineers who were never present for the original prompt session—predictable failure stages follow [[74]](#reference-74):

1. **Velocity spike:** The prototype produces fluent responses on two or three happy-path examples, creating executive pressure to ship immediately.
2. **Consistency erosion:** Different prompts, ad hoc few-shot examples, and implicit assumptions accumulate across sessions; naming conventions, policy interpretations, and action boundaries drift [[50]](#reference-50), [[74]](#reference-74).
3. **Review fatigue:** Because the system has no machine-checkable acceptance contract, human reviewers must read every generated paragraph and trace every tool call from scratch to spot subtle errors.
4. **Incident acceleration:** Hidden assumptions, excessive tool permissions, stale policy citations, and cross-tenant edge cases slip past fatigued reviewers into production [[37]](#reference-37), [[74]](#reference-74).
5. **Velocity collapse:** Trust erodes; every prompt edit breaks a previously working behavior, and engineers spend more time firefighting regressions than building capabilities.

The antidote to unstructured prompting is **steered, specification-driven agent engineering** [[37]](#reference-37), [[50]](#reference-50), [[74]](#reference-74). In a spec-driven workflow, humans define the formal boundaries—the task contract, domain glossary, authority scopes, negative constraints, and acceptance tests—before connecting an autonomous loop [[37]](#reference-37), [[50]](#reference-50). The specification connects business and product intent [[5]](#reference-5), [[41]](#reference-41), [[99]](#reference-99) to developer APIs [[1]](#reference-1), [[3]](#reference-3), enterprise governance [[2]](#reference-2), [[8]](#reference-8), runtime enforcement guards, and deterministic evaluation suites.

| Dimension | Unstructured “Vibe” Prompting | Steered, Contract-Driven Agent Engineering |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Source of truth** | Ephemeral chat history and ad hoc system-prompt edits [[74]](#reference-74) | Versioned, one-page task contract paired with durable rules and schemas [[37]](#reference-37), [[50]](#reference-50) |
| **Definition of success** | Output “looks right” to the developer on 2–3 manual tries | Observable environment postconditions and structured rubric criteria [[37]](#reference-37), [[99]](#reference-99) |
| **Authority & tenancy** | Stated in prose (“Only access Cedar records”) | Enforced by server-bound `Principal` and database query predicates [[2]](#reference-2), [[37]](#reference-37) |
| **Ambiguity & rule conflicts** | Model guesses silently to appear helpful [[50]](#reference-50) | Runtime protocol forces the agent to stop, log the conflict, and escalate [[50]](#reference-50) |
| **Token & context discipline** | Everything is dumped into one growing prompt until context rots [[50]](#reference-50) | Core intent stays compact; specialized reference data is loaded on demand [[50]](#reference-50) |
| **Change management** | Tweaking wording to fix one bug silently breaks three other cases | Contract, tool schemas, and the 20 starter scenarios are versioned together [[37]](#reference-37), [[74]](#reference-74) |

For Northstar, the difference between “help the customer with their export” and “investigate ticket `T-104` under `Cedar` read scope and prepare a reviewable `OPEN` → `INVESTIGATED` proposal grounded in active policy” is the difference between a demo toy and an operable subsystem. Specifications do not try to scripting the exact English sentences the model will write; instead, they constrain the **meaning, evidence, authority, and state transitions** that any acceptable run must satisfy.

## Begin with an observable outcome and product KPIs

A specification should define the desired terminal state of the environment before it says a word about the agent's persona or reasoning style [[37]](#reference-37), [[99]](#reference-99). In *The Art of AI Product Development*, Lipenkova shows how product teams translate high-level business objectives into concrete capability requirements by mapping an **AI opportunity tree** down to measurable user and system outcomes [[99]](#reference-99). If Northstar's support organization wants to reduce mean time to resolution (MTTR) on recurring export failures without increasing policy-citation errors or unauthorized account changes, those product goals must translate directly into observable engineering postconditions [[5]](#reference-5), [[41]](#reference-41), [[99]](#reference-99).

For Northstar's ticket investigator, a run on a standard row-limit ticket is successful when the system:
1. Identifies the affected ticket (`T-104`), account (`A-17`), and export job (`X-58`) within the authenticated tenant (`Cedar`).
2. Retrieves the policy version that was actually in force for the account's current plan (`Standard` → `P-STD-2`, effective `2026-08-01`, `10,000` rows), explicitly distinguishing it from superseded policies (`P-STD-1`, `20,000` rows) and other plan tiers (`Pro` → `P-PRO-1`, `100,000` rows).
3. Grounds its diagnosis in the observed job telemetry (`18,432` rows, error `E_LIMIT_ROWS`).
4. Prepares a concise, accurate `draft_reply` that explains the cause and suggests supported remedies (such as splitting or filtering the export below `10,000` rows) without promising excluded actions.
5. Either stops at `needs_approval` with an immutable, digest-bound proposal ready for a human reviewer, or—when the scenario lacks required evidence or permissions—cleanly abstains, asks for clarification, or escalates without mutating business state.

Notice that the right terminal state depends on the initial condition of the scenario. When a user forgets to supply a ticket ID, asking a clarifying question is a **100% correct outcome**. When a caller under tenant `Cedar` attempts to inspect a `Juniper` record, rejecting the lookup with `not_found_or_not_authorized` is a **100% correct outcome**. When a ticket has already been moved to `INVESTIGATED` or `CLOSED` by another engineer, refusing to overwrite it with a stale proposal is a **100% correct outcome**.

A binary “resolved / unresolved” counter erases these vital distinctions [[37]](#reference-37), [[99]](#reference-99). To prevent your metrics from rewarding reckless guessing—or, conversely, from rewarding an agent that lazily escalates every ticket—track two orthogonal rates from day one:
- **Behavioral correctness (contract compliance rate):** Did the system obey every read/write boundary, cite only valid evidence, and reach the scenario's required terminal state (whether proposal, clarification, or refusal)?
- **Autonomous completion rate (within eligible scope):** On scenarios where sufficient authorized evidence existed to prepare a valid proposal, what fraction did the system complete to a verified, review-ready proposal without human rescue?

Wherever possible, anchor these metrics in the target state of the service rather than in the model's conversational claim [[1]](#reference-1), [[3]](#reference-3). In Northstar, a ticket update is verified when `SELECT status, version, draft_reply FROM tickets WHERE tenant='Cedar' AND id='T-104'` returns `status='INVESTIGATED'` and `version=2` alongside a matching row in `commits`. A model message that says “I have updated the ticket for you” is merely an unverified string until the database transaction commits.

## The one-page Northstar task contract

A task contract is an engineering interface specification between product owners, software developers, security reviewers, and operations leads [[2]](#reference-2), [[8]](#reference-8), [[37]](#reference-37). If a contract spans forty pages of prose, nobody reads it and nobody keeps it updated. If it fits on a single structured page, disagreements surface immediately during design review.

The following table defines the complete v1 task contract for the Northstar support investigator:

| Contract field | Northstar v1 specification | Enforcement mechanism in companion (`northstar.py`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Job statement** | Investigate an export failure and prepare a support response grounded in authorized tenant records | System instructions + tool vocabulary + acceptance rubric |
| **Trigger** | Authenticated support invocation supplying a `ticket_id` (or free-text inquiry requiring clarification) | CLI `demo`/`live` entry point or `run_agent(..., ticket_id=...)` |
| **Principal** | Server-constructed, immutable `Principal(tenant, user, scopes)` derived from authenticated session | `@dataclass(frozen=True) class Principal` (`INVESTIGATOR` vs `REVIEWER`) |
| **Authorized inputs** | `tickets`, `accounts`, `exports`, and effective-dated `policies` belonging to `principal.tenant` | SQLite queries parameterized by `(principal.tenant, value)` |
| **Read boundary** | Requires `"read"` scope; zero cross-tenant disclosure (`Cedar` vs `Juniper`); returns `not_found_or_not_authorized` on miss | `principal.require("read")` and `WHERE tenant=? AND id=?` |
| **Proposal boundary** | Requires `"propose"` scope; targets an `OPEN` ticket at exact `expected_version`; writes only to `proposals` | `store.propose(...)` with SHA-256 `digest` and 900s `expires` |
| **Commit boundary** | Requires `"commit"`, `"approve"`, and `"read"` scopes; human reviewer must match `approval["reviewer"]` and `digest` | `store.commit(...)` inside `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction |
| **Permitted mutation** | Transition `tickets.status` from `'OPEN'` to `'INVESTIGATED'`, store `draft_reply`, increment `version` by `1` | `UPDATE tickets SET status=?, draft_reply=?, version=version+1 WHERE ...` |
| **Excluded effects** | Sending external email, changing account plans, issuing refunds, altering policy limits, or retrying export jobs | Omitted from `TOOL_FIELDS`; rejected by `dispatch` and `store.commit` |
| **Evidence contract** | Snapshot of `account`, `export`, and active `policy` (`P-STD-2` effective `2026-08-01`) hashed into proposal `digest` | `store.evidence(principal, ticket)` re-verified at commit time |
| **Resource budgets** | `max_steps=8`, `max_seconds=60`, per-call timeout `≤ 30s`, `request_bytes <= 24000`, `max_total_tokens=75000` | Enforced in `run_agent` loop before and after every model turn |
| **Accountable owners** | Support Product Owner (domain rules & escalation queue) and Agent Platform Lead (runtime & on-call) | Named operational ownership and incident runbook (Ch. 10, Ch. 13) |

Look closely at how this contract treats **identity and tenancy** [[2]](#reference-2), [[37]](#reference-37). None of the five tools in `TOOL_FIELDS` (`read_ticket`, `read_account`, `read_export`, `read_policy`, `propose_update`) accepts a `tenant` argument from the language model. If the model tries to hallucinate or inject `{"ticket_id": "T-104", "tenant": "Juniper"}`, the dispatcher immediately raises `BoundaryError("unknown_tool_or_invalid_fields")` because `set(args) != set(TOOL_FIELDS[name])`. Tool arguments name the *target object* (`"T-104"`); trusted server state supplies the *authority context* (`principal.tenant = "Cedar"`). Keeping claims and authority in separate channels eliminates an entire class of confused-deputy vulnerabilities before the database is even queried.

## Durable rules, glossary precision, and token-efficient specifications

When specifications are translated into standing instructions for an agent—whether in a `SYSTEM` prompt, a project-root `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md` file, or conditional skill definitions—teams quickly encounter what Volkhover calls **the rules trap** [[50]](#reference-50). Every time the agent makes an unexpected mistake, a developer adds another paragraph of defensive English to the system prompt. Within two months, the standing instructions bloat to thousands of tokens, riding along on every single turn of every conversation.

In *Agentic Spec-Driven Development*, Volkhover identifies three compounding failures caused by bloated, unindexed instruction files [[50]](#reference-50):
1. **Per-turn token tax and context rot:** Because an agent loop is stateless on the model side, standing rules and tool schemas are re-transmitted on every turn [[50]](#reference-50), [[59]](#reference-59).
