A responsible release requires an explicit eligibility boundary, a concrete permission map for autonomy, staffed escalation capacity, a clean way to turn post-launch feedback and policy documentation updates ([[78]](#reference-78)) into verified improvements without contaminating production memory, and an evidence packet that separates proven guarantees from unexecuted plans.

Use the pilot, governance, and release framework in this chapter as an executable blueprint for your own production decisions. As throughout the book, Northstar is a fictional teaching system: no live production pilot, user adoption study, or measured financial ROI is reported here. The templates, queueing calculations, and governance matrices below give you the exact structure needed to run and govern a real launch honestly.

## Launch a bounded capability

State your initial production capability in a single, falsifiable sentence [[99]](#reference-99):
> *"Northstar v1 investigates eligible `Cedar`-format `E_LIMIT_ROWS` support tickets using authorized read-only account, export, and policy records, and prepares a cited diagnostic draft and status-update proposal for human analyst review."*

In Stage 1 of a launch, the capability can run purely as a **read-and-draft assistant** with zero automated ticket writes. Once the pilot cohort validates diagnostic accuracy, citation usability, and operational stability, Stage 2 can enable the **bound-approval commit path** (`OPEN` → `INVESTIGATED`) after verifying the action-path suite (`29 checks`) and rollback rehearsal (Chapter 13).

Make your **exclusion list** just as concrete and visible as your feature list [[45]](#reference-45), [[65]](#reference-65). Northstar v1 does **not**:
- Send external emails or messages directly to customers.
- Modify subscription plans (`A-17`), alter row quotas, or issue billing credits.
- Repair, split, or re-run failed data exports (`X-58`).
- Claim in a draft that an export was repaired when only an investigation occurred.

These exclusions are not legalistic fine print buried in documentation; they define the hard perimeter of the service in both the runtime dispatcher and the supervision UI [[45]](#reference-45).

Enforce **task eligibility** deterministically at intake before invoking a language model [[65]](#reference-65), [[99]](#reference-99). An incoming ticket is eligible for Northstar v1 only if:
1. It belongs to an enabled pilot tenant (`Cedar`) with verified principal authority.
2. It resolves to an identifiable account (`A-17`) and export failure record (`X-58` with `E_LIMIT_ROWS`).
3. It falls within the evaluated export-limit task family rather than requesting custom legal exceptions, schema migrations, or unrecognized error codes.

When an incoming ticket falls outside those eligibility predicates—or when required historical records are unavailable—the intake router immediately directs the ticket to the standard human support workflow with a clear reason code (`INELIGIBLE_TASK_FAMILY` or `MISSING_REQUIRED_RECORDS`). An agent runtime must never quietly expand its own product scope in production just because a novel ticket arrived in the queue [[98]](#reference-98), [[99]](#reference-99).

## Choose a pilot cohort that answers the product question

A pilot is a controlled scientific and operational experiment in production, not a ceremonial preview for executives [[43]](#reference-43), [[99]](#reference-99). Select a pilot cohort that genuinely exercises the work you intend to improve while bounding blast radius if an unexpected failure occurs [[65]](#reference-65), [[99]](#reference-99):
- **Representative users, not just the agent's authors**: If the only people testing the pilot are the machine learning engineers who wrote the prompts, they will instinctively work around UI friction and spot subtle policy hallucinations that an ordinary support analyst under queue pressure might miss. Recruit a small, named group of domain analysts with documented baseline metrics and direct communication channels to the engineering team.
- **Representative task distribution (ordinary volume + supported edge cases)**: Do not cherry-pick only trivial tickets where every field is clean just to manufacture a `99%` pilot success slide. Include the routine `E_LIMIT_ROWS` volume (`18,432` rows vs. `10,000` rows under `P-STD-2`) *and* a monitored sample of temporal boundary cases (such as downgraded accounts around the `2026-08-01` transition from `P-STD-1` to `P-STD-2`). Keep unsupported task families out of autonomous execution, but count how frequently they arrive at intake—if `85%` of real support tickets are ineligible, your bounded scope may be safe but commercially too narrow [[41]](#reference-41), [[99]](#reference-99).
- **One primary decision question**: Frame the pilot around a concrete hypothesis: *Does Northstar reduce total human handling effort per verified ticket resolution while preserving 100% of our authority gates and meeting our factual accuracy bar for the `Cedar` pilot cohort?* [[41]](#reference-41), [[42]](#reference-42).

| Pilot Design Dimension | Northstar v1 Pilot Specification | Operational Evidence Collected | Failure Mode if Omitted |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Eligible user cohort** | Named group of 4–6 `Cedar` support analysts across shifts | Analyst experience level, shift load, baseline handling speed | Engineers test their own tool and miss real workflow friction |
| **Eligible task scope** | `E_LIMIT_ROWS` export tickets (`T-104` family) with linked `account_id` and `export_id` | Intake eligibility rate, exclusion reasons, task-family mix | Agent attempts arbitrary billing/bug tickets and hallucinates |
| **Initial autonomy tier** | Stage 1: Read & draft only → Stage 2: Bound-approval ticket commit | Tool calls executed, proposal states, zero unapproved writes | Premature write automation mutates tickets on flawed drafts |
| **Baseline comparison** | Existing manual analyst triage and template workflow on comparable cohort | End-to-end resolution time, factual error rate, edit distance | Claiming "AI saved time" without measuring review/rework overhead |
| **Supervision rule** | 100% human analyst review and bound approval before any commit | Review duration, rejection reasons, citation clicks, heavy edits | Silent drift or rubber-stamping (`illusion of competence`) |
| **Escalation path** | Named support lead (domain) + on-call engineer (runtime) | Escalation rate, queue wait time, time-to-resolution | Unresolved tasks pile up in a dead-end "Needs Review" bucket |
| **Exposure volume gate** | Minimum 200 reviewed eligible tasks across all active families (not just 14 calendar days) | Sample count per task family (`ordinary`, `temporal_conflict`, `missing_data`) | Declaring victory after 2 weeks when only 8 tickets actually ran |
| **Pre-declared exit gate** | Expand to Stage 2/next tenant, revise & re-run, narrow scope, or halt | Signed evaluation packet comparing observed SLIs to pre-set thresholds | Moving goalposts post-hoc to justify launching a weak system |

Notice the distinction in **Exposure volume gate**: calendar time is not sample size [[43]](#reference-43). Running a two-week pilot over a quiet holiday period where only twelve routine tickets arrive provides zero statistical evidence about how the system handles `P-STD-1` vs. `P-STD-2` policy conflicts. Gate pilot progression on **completed, reviewed task exposure across each target family**, supplemented by controlled fault-injection drills (Chapter 13) for rare failure modes.

## Make autonomy a set of permissions, not a marketing slider

Industry commentary often describes agent autonomy as a single numerical dial from "Level 1 (Copilot)" to "Level 5 (Fully Autonomous)." In enterprise systems engineering, a single autonomy number is useless because an agent's permissions vary independently across discovery, context selection, tool reading, proposal drafting, state mutation, and external communication [[2]](#reference-2), [[65]](#reference-65), [[98]](#reference-98).

Define autonomy as an explicit **Permission & Supervision Map** bound to each Release Stage [[65]](#reference-65), [[98]](#reference-98):

| Capability Dimension | Stage 1: Supervised Diagnostic Draft | Stage 2: Bound-Approval Internal Commit | Stage 3: Scoped Routine Automation (Optional / Conditional) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Trigger & Intake** | Analyst-initiated click on `T-104` | Analyst-initiated or deduplicated `EXPORT_FAILED` event (`X-58`) | Deduplicated event on verified routine cohort |
| **Read Authority** | Autonomous read of `Cedar` `read_ticket`, `read_account`, `read_export`, `read_policy` | Same tenant-scoped read allowlist | Same tenant-scoped read allowlist |
| **Ambiguity / Missing Evidence (`X-58` date missing)** | Must abstain and list missing fields in draft | Must transition to `UNRESOLVED_EVIDENCE` and escalate to human | Must immediately exit automation path to human queue |
| **Internal Ticket State Update (`OPEN` → `INVESTIGATED`)** | **Prohibited** (analyst copies/applies draft manually) | **Permitted ONLY with bound human approval**, current evidence re-check, and receipt verification | Permitted *only* for deterministic single-policy match if organization formally authorizes; exceptions require bound approval |
| **External Customer Messaging** | **Prohibited** | **Prohibited** | **Prohibited** (requires separate review & release packet) |
| **Account Plan / Billing Mutation (`A-17`)** | **Prohibited** | **Prohibited** | **Prohibited** |

As Babak Hodjat emphasizes in *The Agentic Enterprise* [[98]](#reference-98), enterprise autonomy expands incrementally by **earning trust on narrow, auditable action families**, never by flipping a global switch from supervised to unsupervised. Moreover, Stage 3 (automated internal tagging on routine deterministic matches) is **never an obligatory destination**. In many regulated support, legal, medical, and financial workflows [[63]](#reference-63), [[83]](#reference-83), [[98]](#reference-98), Stage 2—where the agent eliminates 80% of the tedious evidence-gathering labor across `T-104`, `A-17`, `X-58`, and `P-STD-2` while a human professional retains final sign-off authority—is the optimal permanent operating state.

Remember also that **user comfort is not evidence of safety** [[45]](#reference-45). After two weeks of seeing accurate drafts, busy analysts will naturally ask: *"Can you just add an 'Auto-Approve All' checkbox so I don't have to read these?"* Yielding to that request without independent evidence that the agent handles exceptions safely removes your primary safety barrier right as task volume scales. Changes to the autonomy permission map belong to accountable engineering, domain, and security owners—not individual user convenience toggles.

## Set success and stop criteria before the pilot starts

Write down the quantitative and qualitative rules that govern your pilot **before** inspecting the first pilot run [[43]](#reference-43), [[99]](#reference-99). When teams wait until the end of a pilot to define success, confirmation bias takes over: if accuracy is high but handling time increased, the team declares it a "quality pilot"; if accuracy is mediocre but drafts are fast, the team declares it a "speed pilot."

Separate **hard stop criteria (immediate containment gates)** from **product value & quality thresholds (cohort decision gates)** [[43]](#reference-43), [[65]](#reference-65), [[99]](#reference-99):

| Pilot Signal Observed | Pre-Declared Operational Decision | Rationale & Required Follow-Up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Any confirmed cross-tenant disclosure (`Cedar` ↔ `Juniper`) or unapproved mutation** | **Immediate Halt (Kill Switch)**: Disable runtime capability and open Severity-1 incident | Hard boundary failure; cannot be "averaged out" by fast drafts on other tickets |
| **2. Stale-policy citation (`P-STD-1` `20,000` rows applied as current post-`2026-08-01`) exceeds threshold** | **Pause & Fix Retrieval/Contract**: Halt pilot expansion; inspect policy metadata and verifier gate | Core domain competence failure on temporal applicability |
| **3. Total analyst handling time (review + edit + rework) exceeds manual baseline** | **Redesign Supervision or Draft Scope**: Do not expand cohort | The system is shifting cognitive load onto reviewers rather than saving work [[41]](#reference-41), [[42]](#reference-42), [[45]](#reference-45) |
| **4. Escalation queue wait time breaches staffed SLA** | **Throttle Intake / Disable Event Triggers**: Restrict to analyst-initiated runs | Unstaffed human fallback breaks the end-to-end service promise |
| **5. Cohort Cost per Verified Resolution exceeds FinOps budget** | **Optimize Critical Path / Tiered Routing (Ch. 14)**: Remove redundant turns or narrow eligible cohort | Unit economics must include failed runs, retries, and human review labor |
| **6. Strong performance on single-policy cases; high error rate on plan-downgrade edge cases** | **Narrow Release Scope**: Ship for single-policy cohort; route downgrade edge cases deterministically to humans | Honest scope narrowing captures proven value while containing unproven risk [[99]](#reference-99) |
| **7. Zero hard-gate violations + met quality bar + verified net reduction in handling effort** | **Approve Controlled Progression**: Advance to next stage or next tenant cohort with updated manifest | Expansion is earned by recorded evidence packet |

Adapting the error-budget and release governance mindset from *The Site Reliability Workbook* [[43]](#reference-43) to AI products [[41]](#reference-41), [[42]](#reference-42), [[99]](#reference-99) means treating **scope narrowing** (Row 6) and **stopping** as successful engineering decisions rather than personal defeats. Shipping a rock-solid agent for routine `E_LIMIT_ROWS` tickets while routing complex multi-contract disputes to senior specialists delivers immediate operational value without risking customer trust.

## Staff the human path and model review capacity

Every human-in-the-loop architecture is also a **human queueing system** [[43]](#reference-43), [[65]](#reference-65). If an agent generates proposals and escalations faster than human supervisors can review them, the review queue grows without bound, proposals go stale while waiting (`A-17`'s state or `T-104`'s version changes underneath the pending proposal!), and stressed reviewers begin rubber-stamping approvals just to clear their backlog.

Perform explicit **review-capacity arithmetic** before enabling intake [[43]](#reference-43), [[65]](#reference-65):
- Suppose eligible `Cedar` tickets arrive at an average rate of `λ = 30 tasks/hour`.
- Suppose `80%` (`24 tasks/hour`) produce a clean reviewable proposal requiring an average of `t_review = 2.0 minutes` of active analyst verification (checking `X-58`'s `18,432` rows against `P-STD-2`'s `10,000` rows and `2026-08-01` effective date), while `20%` (`6 tasks/hour`) escalate as `UNRESOLVED_EVIDENCE` or require draft rework averaging `t_escalate = 8.0 minutes` of deep manual investigation.
- **Total human supervision demand per hour**:
  ```
  W_human = (24 × 2.0) + (6 × 8.0) = 48.0 + 48.0 = 96.0 staff-minutes per hour (1.60 full-time equivalent analysts)
  ```
- Even if you had `0%` escalations (`30 × 2.0 = 60 minutes/hour`), queueing theory (`M/M/c` / Pollaczek–Khinchine formula) proves that operating a human reviewer at `ρ = 100%` utilization (`60 minutes of work per 60-minute hour`) causes queue wait times to approach infinity whenever arrivals cluster! Accounting for a safe target utilization ceiling of `ρ ≤ 0.70–0.75`, breaks, shift handoffs, and arrival variance, supporting `96 staff-minutes/hour` of supervision and escalation work requires at least `⌈ 1.60 / 0.70 ⌉ = 3` trained analysts on shift.

Look at how sensitive this staffing math is to the **escalation rate**: if a faulty policy ingestion doubles the escalation rate from `20%` (`6 tasks/hour`) to `40%` (`12 tasks/hour`), human demand jumps to `(18 × 2.0) + (12 × 8.0) = 36 + 96 = 132 staff-minutes/hour`, immediately overwhelming a two-person shift.

Design every escalation handoff so the human analyst never starts from zero [[45]](#reference-45):
1. Display the exact **structured evidence already verified** (`T-104`, `A-17`, `X-58` with `18,432` rows and `E_LIMIT_ROWS`).
2. Highlight the **exact reason for escalation** (`"Missing event_time on X-58; cannot disambiguate P-STD-1 (20,000 rows) vs. P-STD-2 (10,000 rows effective 2026-08-01)"`).
3. Confirm the **current state and action receipt ledger** (`"No changes committed to T-104; status remains OPEN"`).
4. Route distinctly by failure type: domain policy ambiguities go to senior support leads; runtime tool timeouts or lease failures go to the on-call platform engineer.

## Assign ownership, package for distribution, and govern the agentic enterprise

In traditional software, behavior changes only when an engineer merges code and deploys a binary. In an agentic system, production behavior can shift on a Tuesday afternoon because a product manager edited a prompt template, a compliance officer uploaded policy `P-STD-2` (`10,000` rows effective `2026-08-01`), a vendor updated a floating model alias, or an infrastructure team changed an MCP server timeout [[2]](#reference-2), [[65]](#reference-65), [[98]](#reference-98). If everything is owned by a vague, collective `"AI Team,"` then nothing is owned when an incident occurs [[29]](#reference-29), [[98]](#reference-98).

Establish explicit **component ownership and change-review gates** across the organization [[2]](#reference-2), [[29]](#reference-29), [[65]](#reference-65), [[98]](#reference-98):

| Behavioral Component | Accountable Owner Role | Mandatory Change-Review Gate Before Production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Product scope, eligibility, & ROI** [[41]](#reference-41), [[42]](#reference-42), [[99]](#reference-99) | Product Owner | Cohort eligibility review, handling-time baseline comparison, sunset criteria |
| **Domain policies & escalation rules (`P-STD-2`)** | Domain / Support Operations Lead | Effective-date metadata check (`2026-08-01`), contradiction audit, GEO formatting [[78]](#reference-78) |
| **Runtime, state store, leases, & tools** | Lead Systems / Agent Engineer | 100% pass on deterministic `29 checks` + MCP boundary tests (`test_mcp.py`) |
| **Prompts, instruction packs, & routing rules** | Named Behavior / Applied AI Owner | Version hash bump + full Chapter 8 scenario evaluation across all task families |
| **Retrieval corpus, indexing, & retention** | Data / Knowledge Engineer | Tenant scope verification (`Cedar` vs. `Juniper`), provenance tags, TTL deletion |
| **Evaluation suite, rubrics, & holdout sets** | Evaluation / QA Owner | Leakage audit, rubric calibration with domain practitioners, regression coverage |
| **Deployment, SLIs, queues, & incident response** | SRE / Platform Operations Lead | Rollback rehearsal (Ch. 13), lease drain test, paging threshold calibration [[43]](#reference-43) |
| **Identity, authority, & threat boundaries** | Security Engineer + Systems Lead | Confused-deputy / token audit, prompt-injection red-teaming, kill-switch verification |
| **Supervision UI & accessibility** [[45]](#reference-45), [[46]](#reference-46) | Design / Frontend Owner | Cognitive-load review (Ch. 15), keyboard ergonomics, honest status states |

When distributing an agentic solution across multiple business units or external enterprise tenants, Soh, Tidwell, and Singh (*Building and Distributing Agentic AI Solutions* [[65]](#reference-65)) and Hodjat (*The Agentic Enterprise* [[98]](#reference-98)) highlight three packaging requirements that separate an internal prototype from a distributable enterprise product:
1. **Per-tenant configuration, entitlement, and isolation packaging**: Package each tenant onboarding (`Cedar`, `Juniper`) as a declarative profile specifying enabled task families, autonomy stage (Stage 1 vs. Stage 2), `cache_salt` and database partition keys, rate/cost quotas (`AgentBudget`), and regional data-residency bindings [[65]](#reference-65).
2. **Metering aligned with verified value, not raw failed retries**: Whether allocating internal chargebacks across departments or pricing an external B2B product, align metering with **eligible runs or verified outcomes** within agreed service-level objectives [[53]](#reference-53), [[65]](#reference-65), rather than billing customers extra when your own internal tool retries loop.
3. **Proportional change governance**: Route changes by their **behavioral blast radius**, not by file extension [[98]](#reference-98). Fixing a typo in a UI label is a trivial change; editing two words in an instruction pack that alters when `propose_update` escalates is a behavioral release requiring the same evaluation gate as a code change.

## Learn from feedback and structure authoritative knowledge (GEO)

Once Northstar is live with the `Cedar` pilot cohort, every analyst interaction generates valuable operational signals: analysts approve proposals, edit draft phrasing, reject incorrect diagnoses, or abandon a run and switch back to manual triage [[45]](#reference-45), [[99]](#reference-99). How you capture that feedback—and how you structure your authoritative domain documents so retrieval systems and models interpret them accurately—determines whether the system improves safely or drifts into chaos.

### Feedback is an audited signal for engineering review, not automatic weight training
Avoid two opposite mistakes when handling user feedback [[45]](#reference-45), [[99]](#reference-99):
- **Never wire user edits or thumbs-up/down clicks directly into live shared memory or automatic weight updates**: Users are fallible, rushed, and sometimes misinformed themselves. If one analyst mistakenly edits a draft on `T-104` to say *"Your Standard limit is 20,000 rows (`P-STD-1`)"* after `2026-08-01`, and your system automatically ingests user edits as "learned domain facts" into a global RAG memory bank, that single human error immediately poisons future runs across the entire `Cedar` tenant!
- **Capture structured feedback reason codes linked to the exact artifact hash**: When an analyst edits or rejects a proposal, prompt for a lightweight, low-friction reason tag (`WRONG_POLICY_VERSION`, `MISSING_ACCOUNT_CONTEXT`, `TONE_TOO_VERBOSE`, `INCORRECT_ACTION_SCOPE`) alongside the diff between the original proposal and the analyst's final version.
- **Route recurring feedback patterns to the right architectural layer**:
  - If analysts repeatedly trim three paragraphs of generic export advice → tighten the output schema and prompt instructions (Behavior Owner).
  - If the agent repeatedly misses a plan downgrade timestamp → add the downgrade timestamp field directly to the `read_account` tool payload (Engineering Owner) and add a regression scenario to the evaluation suite (Evaluation Owner).
  - If the organization later decides to use curated, expert-verified trajectories for LoRA/DPO fine-tuning (Chapter 14 [[75]](#reference-75)), treat that dataset through a formal data-governance, PII-redaction, and release-evaluation pipeline—and communicate honestly to users that flagging a bad draft files an engineering defect rather than instantaneously retraining the live model [[45]](#reference-45).

### Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) for authoritative policy and product documentation
Why do both internal enterprise RAG agents and external AI search engines so frequently cite outdated policy limits (such as citing `P-STD-1`'s `20,000`-row limit after `P-STD-2`'s `10,000`-row limit took effect on `2026-08-01`)? Often, the root cause is not model reasoning failure—it is poorly structured source documentation!

In *Generative Engine Optimization* [[78]](#reference-78), Ross Hudgens shows how generative retrieval systems extract, chunk, rank, and synthesize claims from documents. Applying those structural principles to your organization's internal and public policy documentation dramatically improves retrieval accuracy and citation trustworthiness:
1. **Self-contained semantic chunks with explicit temporal & entity headers**: When a chunker splits a 20-page PDF into 400-token passages, a table row reading `| Standard | 20,000 rows |` divorced from the page-1 title `"Archived 2025 Policy (Superseded)"` looks identical to current policy! Repeat the canonical document identifier, status, and effective dates in every section heading and table caption: e.g., `### Policy P-STD-2 (STATUS: ACTIVE | Effective: 2026-08-01 | Supersedes: P-STD-1): Standard Plan Export Limit = 10,000 Rows` [[78]](#reference-78).
2. **Explicit tombstone and supersession markers on historical documents**: Never leave old policy pages (`P-STD-1`) floating in documentation portals with present-tense verbs (`"The Standard plan allows 20,000 rows"`). Prepend an explicit machine- and human-readable supersession banner (`status: SUPERSEDED_BY_P_STD_2_ON_2026_08_01`) and rewrite historical summaries in explicit past tense with closed date intervals (`effective 2025-01-01 through 2026-07-31`).
3. **Canonical, disambiguated factual tables over buried prose**: Generative engines and RAG retrievers extract structured key-value tables and explicit FAQ blocks far more reliably than numbers buried in dense narrative paragraphs [[78]](#reference-78). Publish a single authoritative policy changelog table mapping each plan tier, policy ID (`P-STD-1`, `P-STD-2`), exact row limit (`20,000` vs. `10,000`), error code (`E_LIMIT_ROWS`), and effective date (`2026-08-01`).

## Treat adoption as evidence of fit, not proof of correctness

As Janna Lipenkova emphasizes in *The Art of AI Product Development* [[99]](#reference-99)—alongside Nika [[41]](#reference-41), Granados [[42]](#reference-42), Wooten [[13]](#reference-13), and Greenwald and Kahn [[14]](#reference-14)—shipping an AI capability requires continuously diagnosing the two-by-two relationship between **user adoption (workflow fit)** and **domain correctness (verified quality)**:

- **High Adoption + High Verified Correctness**: Genuine product-market and workflow fit. The agent saves real handling effort on `T-104`-class tickets while upholding every policy and authority invariant.
- **Low Adoption + High Verified Correctness**: Workflow friction, latency, or trust gap [[45]](#reference-45), [[46]](#reference-46), [[99]](#reference-99). The diagnosis of `X-58` (`18,432` rows vs. `P-STD-2` `10,000` rows) is accurate, but perhaps the analyst has to open a separate browser tab, wait 30 seconds synchronously, or copy-paste six fields manually, making their existing keyboard macro faster. Fix the integration ergonomics and async pre-investigation trigger (Chapter 13) rather than changing the model.
- **High Adoption + Low Verified Correctness (The Dangerous Trap)**: **Automation complacency and perverse incentives** [[42]](#reference-42), [[45]](#reference-45), [[89]](#reference-89). Analysts are using the tool heavily—perhaps because management mandated AI usage metrics or because clicking "Approve" clears their queue faster—while subtle factual errors (`P-STD-1` vs. `P-STD-2` mix-ups or unverified claims) slip through into customer tickets. High adoption here is a warning siren, not a success metric!
- **Low Adoption + Low Verified Correctness**: Fundamental task or capability mismatch. Narrow the scope to a tractable sub-problem or sunset the capability cleanly [[99]](#reference-99).

Always evaluate the agent against the **real baseline alternative** [[13]](#reference-13), [[14]](#reference-14), [[41]](#reference-41). If a ten-line deterministic UI script that displays `account.plan`, `export.rows` (`18,432`), and `policy.max_rows` (`10,000` as of `2026-08-01`) right at the top of the ticket screen solves 80% of the analyst's problem in `50 milliseconds` at zero LLM cost, ship that deterministic UI improvement first and reserve the agent for complex multi-record investigations where flexible synthesis genuinely adds value [[42]](#reference-42), [[99]](#reference-99).

## Reduce autonomy or sunset cleanly when the evidence changes

In a living enterprise environment, a capability that was safe and cost-effective in August can become unsafe or uneconomical in November—even if not a single line of Northstar's Python code changed [[43]](#reference-43), [[98]](#reference-98), [[99]](#reference-99). A newly launched product tier introduces complex contract riders that the retrieval index does not cover; support staffing drops during a reorganization so the approval queue backs up; or an upstream model provider deprecates a pinned model snapshot.

Your operating plan must treat **autonomy reduction (de-escalation)** as a routine, well-rehearsed control mechanism rather than an improvised panic maneuver [[43]](#reference-43), [[65]](#reference-65), [[98]](#reference-98):
1. **Multi-level runtime kill switches and scope throttles**: Build configuration toggles enforced directly inside the server dispatcher and worker loop (never just hiding a button in the frontend CSS!):
   - *Toggle A*: Pause automated event triggers (`EXPORT_FAILED`) while keeping analyst-initiated runs active.
   - *Toggle B*: Downgrade from Stage 2 (bound-approval commit enabled) back to Stage 1 (read-and-draft only) by disabling `commit_update` in the dispatcher.
   - *Toggle C*: Narrow the intake eligibility filter to exclude a regressing task subfamily or tenant.
   - *Toggle D*: Full service pause—stop claiming new worker jobs, drain active leases safely, and route 100% of tickets to the manual baseline workflow.
2. **Explicit handling of in-flight runs and pending approvals during downgrade**: Whenever you downgrade autonomy or pause commits, run the same database reconciliation query used in our Chapter 13 rollback rehearsal: identify all runs currently sitting in `awaiting_approval` or `committing`, record their state clearly in the audit log, and notify analysts in the UI whether pending proposals must be applied manually or re-verified.
3. **Responsible capability retirement (sunsetting)** [[99]](#reference-99): If pilot evidence shows that a specialist capability does not clear the value or reliability bar after focused iteration, retire it cleanly. Export required audit logs and action receipts for compliance retention, transition users back to the baseline workflow, revoke service credentials and database tokens, and shut down unused event consumers. Leaving an abandoned "zombie agent" running in the background with active credentials is a severe security liability [[2]](#reference-2), [[98]](#reference-98).

## Prepare for the first incident and communicate with accountability

No matter how thorough your offline checks and pilot gates are, a production system operating in a changing world will eventually encounter an incident [[36]](#reference-36), [[43]](#reference-43), [[45]](#reference-45). The difference between a trustworthy engineering organization and a reckless one is whether the first incident triggers a practiced, accountable recovery or a chaotic blame game [[29]](#reference-29), [[43]](#reference-43).

Before enabling Northstar for any real user cohort, establish four incident-response pillars:
1. **Named Incident Commander and role clarity**: Every person on call knows who owns containment, who inspects the SQLite/database state and receipt ledger, who communicates with support leadership, and which kill switch halts mutations.
2. **Consequence-driven triage and containment**:
   - *Scenario A (Semantic / Policy Drift)*: A formatting bug in a newly ingested policy document causes drafts to cite `P-STD-1` (`20,000` rows) instead of `P-STD-2` (`10,000` rows effective `2026-08-01`). **Action**: Pause new drafts on the affected policy family, query all trace records (`evidence_refs`) that cited `P-STD-1` since the ingestion timestamp, flag any affected tickets for analyst correction, fix the policy metadata, and add a pre-ingestion validation check.
   - *Scenario B (Boundary / Authorization Breach)*: A bug in a newly added adapter leaks a `Juniper` record to a `Cedar` session or commits an update without verifying a current bound approval. **Action**: Trigger full containment (Toggle D), preserve forensic logs and database snapshots, engage security/privacy response, audit every run in the exposure window via the trace store, and do not restore service until the root cause is fixed and verified in the deterministic test suite.
3. **Systemic root-cause remediation over prompt band-aids**: In post-incident review, trace why the defense-in-depth layers missed the defect. Never close an incident action item with *"Added 'IMPORTANT: Do not do X' to the system prompt"* when the failure requires a deterministic code check, a schema constraint, or a database foreign-key invariant.
4. **Honest, clear user communication**: As Greg Nudelman emphasizes in *UX for AI* [[45]](#reference-45), user trust survives errors when the system and team communicate honestly what happened, which records were affected, what was fixed, and what action (if any) the user needs to take—while providing a simple mechanism to correct and override faulty AI outputs.

## Make the release decision from a complete evidence packet

We conclude the book where every production launch decision belongs: assembling the **Release Evidence Packet** [[43]](#reference-43), [[65]](#reference-65), [[98]](#reference-98), [[99]](#reference-99). A release packet is a concise, version-pinned engineering document that connects every claim about the system to verifiable evidence—and explicitly separates **demonstrated results** from **planned or unexecuted work**.

| Release Packet Section | Concrete Artifact in Northstar | What Is Demonstrated in Companion | What Requires Target Environment Execution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Capability & Scope Contract** | Single-sentence capability, eligibility rules, and explicit exclusion list (`16.1`) | Defined for `Cedar` ticket `T-104`, `A-17`, `X-58` (`18,432` rows, `E_LIMIT_ROWS`) | Sign-off by your organization's domain and product owners [[99]](#reference-99) |
| **2. Autonomy Permission Map** | Stage 1 (draft) vs. Stage 2 (bound-approval commit) permission matrix (`16.3`) | Enforced in local runtime dispatcher and `mcp_read_server.py` | Integration with production IAM/OAuth and enterprise RBAC [[65]](#reference-65), [[98]](#reference-98) |
| **3. Deterministic Action & Boundary Suite** | Automated verification of tenant isolation, schema validation, bound approvals, idempotent receipts, and postconditions | **Executed & passing locally**: `29 checks` in offline suite + `test_mcp.py` subprocess check | Continuous execution in your production CI/CD pipeline on every manifest change |
| **4. Scenario Evaluation & Benchmarks** | Held-out task families (`ordinary`, `temporal_conflict` `P-STD-1` vs. `P-STD-2`, `missing_evidence`, `adversarial`) | **200 scenario specifications** defined in companion repository (`Chapter 8`) | Provisioning live model endpoints, reviewing expected rubrics with domain experts, and recording live trial runs |
| **5. Operational, Lease, & Rollback Readiness** | Durable state schema, worker leases, trace redaction, SLIs, and rollback reconciliation (`Chapter 13`) | Local SQLite transactional store and state transitions verified | Production ASGI gateway, backup restore drill, Kubernetes probes [[82]](#reference-82), and executed rollback rehearsal |
| **6. FinOps, Latency, & Staffing Model** | Critical-path decomposition, `AgentBudget` caps, and human review capacity math (`Ch. 14`, `16.5`) | Illustrative sensitivity models and interactive calculator | Measured `p50`/`p95` latencies, actual provider billing rates, and staffed shift schedules [[53]](#reference-53) |
| **7. Component Ownership & Kill Switches** | Named owners for code, prompts, policies, data, evals, ops, and security (`16.6`, `16.9`) | Reference governance table and runtime stop states | Assigned on-call rotation and tested runtime configuration toggles [[29]](#reference-29), [[43]](#reference-43), [[98]](#reference-98) |

Look carefully at Row 3 and Row 4 of this table. Throughout this book, we have maintained an uncompromising distinction between **what code and tests have actually executed** and **what specifications or design templates await your live environment**:
- The companion codebase's deterministic suite of **`29 checks`** and the MCP subprocess test (`python3 test_mcp.py`) are runnable, self-contained, and verified against the synthetic `Cedar` and `Juniper` SQLite fixtures. They prove that the local state machine, tenant filters, schema validators, bound approval checks, idempotent receipts, and postconditions behave as specified.
- The companion's **`200` scenario specifications** provide a structured blueprint for evaluating live models, but their target model environments still need provisioning and their domain expectations must be reviewed for your deployment before claiming live-model benchmark numbers.

When your release review committee meets to inspect this packet, empower them to make one of four explicit engineering decisions based strictly on the evidence ledger:
1. **Launch the bounded capability** to the specified pilot cohort at the approved autonomy stage.
2. **Revise and re-run** a specific failed check, missing rehearsal, or under-powered evaluation family before launching.
3. **Narrow the scope** (for instance, launching Stage 1 draft-only or excluding a task subfamily where exceptions failed) so deployed autonomy matches proven competence.
4. **Stop or defer** the launch if the capability does not clear the safety boundary or net-value bar.

That discipline—earning autonomy step by step through explicit boundaries, verifiable evidence, and operational ownership—is what separates a fragile prototype from a reliable engineering system.

## Exercises and answer guidance

### Exercise 16.1: Specify the operational kill switches and incident containment for Northstar
Draft the exact runtime kill-switch specification and first three containment steps for two distinct synthetic pilot incidents on Northstar:
- **Incident A (Cross-Tenant Boundary Failure)**: A newly deployed retrieval adapter returns a `Juniper` account record during a `Cedar` investigation of `T-104`.
- **Incident B (Policy Ingestion Error)**: A documentation update accidentally strips the `2026-08-01` effective date from `P-STD-2` (`10,000` rows), causing Northstar drafts to cite `P-STD-1` (`20,000` rows) on `18,432`-row `E_LIMIT_ROWS` failures.

Explain why a frontend-only UI toggle is insufficient, how in-flight worker leases and pending approvals (`awaiting_approval`) must be handled in each case, and how you verify whether any ticket was mutated before containment completed.

*Answer guidance*:
- A frontend UI toggle leaves background lease workers, event triggers (`EXPORT_FAILED`), and direct API/MCP endpoints running unprotected; kill switches must be enforced inside the server-side `dispatch` and worker lease loop.
- In **Incident A** (hard security boundary breach), immediately activate Full Service Pause (Toggle D), revoke/terminate active worker leases, invalidate all uncommitted proposals from the affected release manifest, query the trace and receipt store (`action_receipts`) for every run executed under the faulty adapter version to identify any cross-tenant reads or writes, and engage security incident response.
- In **Incident B** (domain data regression), pause automated event triggers and downgrade or block proposals touching `P-STD-1`/`P-STD-2`, query all pending proposals in `awaiting_approval` that cited `P-STD-1` after the bad ingestion timestamp and mark them `INVALIDATED_STALE_POLICY`, restore the `2026-08-01` effective date on `P-STD-2`, and add a pre-ingestion schema check requiring `effective_date` on all active policies.

### Exercise 16.2: Calculate human review staffing under escalation spikes
Using the queueing and staffing model from Section 16.5:
1. Suppose `Cedar` pilot volume increases to `λ = 45 eligible tickets/hour`. On `80%` of tickets (`36 tickets/hour`), the agent produces a clean proposal requiring `t_review = 1.5 minutes` of analyst verification. On the remaining `20%` (`9 tickets/hour`), the run escalates (`UNRESOLVED_EVIDENCE`) or requires manual correction averaging `t_escalate = 7.0 minutes`. Calculate the total human supervision minutes required per hour and the minimum number of analysts needed on shift assuming a maximum sustainable utilization of `ρ = 0.75`.
2. Suppose a product change broadens intake to include unverified billing disputes, causing the escalation rate to jump from `20%` to `50%` (while arrival rate rises to `λ = 60 tickets/hour`). Recompute the required analyst staffing and explain what happens to pending approval freshness (`T-104` / `A-17` state drift) if staffing remains fixed at the Step 1 level.

*Answer guidance*:
1. At `λ = 45`: `W_human = (36 × 1.5) + (9 × 7.0) = 54.0 + 63.0 = 117.0 staff-minutes/hour` (`1.95 hours of work per hour`). At `ρ = 0.75` (`45 productive minutes per analyst-hour`), required staffing is `⌈ 117.0 / 45.0 ⌉ = ⌈ 2.60 ⌉ = 3 analysts on shift`.
2. At `λ = 60` with `50%` escalation (`30` clean, `30` escalated): `W_human = (30 × 1.5) + (30 × 7.0) = 45.0 + 210.0 = 255.0 staff-minutes/hour`, requiring `⌈ 255.0 / 45.0 ⌉ = ⌈ 5.67 ⌉ = 6 analysts`. If only `3` analysts are staffed (capacity `135 min/hr` vs. demand `255 min/hr`, so `ρ = 1.89 > 1`), the review queue grows by `120 staff-minutes` every hour! Proposals sit unreviewed for hours while underlying ticket and account states change, causing massive precondition failures (`E_STALE_EVIDENCE`) at commit time.

## Further reading

**AI Product Strategy, Launch Lifecycle, & Value Measurement**: Janna Lipenkova, *The Art of AI Product Development* [[99]](#reference-99), Marily Nika, *The AI Product Playbook* [[41]](#reference-41), and Granados, *The AI-Powered Product Manager* [[42]](#reference-42), cover problem selection, pilot cohort design, adoption vs. correctness diagnostics, unit-economics validation, and capability sunsetting. Wooten, *Cofounder.AI* [[13]](#reference-13), and Bruce Greenwald and Judd Kahn, *Competition Demystified* [[14]](#reference-14), provide foundational analysis of customer alternatives and durable competitive value.

**Packaging, Distributing, & Governing the Agentic Enterprise**: Julian Soh, Aaron Tidwell, and Priyanshi Singh, *Building and Distributing Agentic AI Solutions* [[65]](#reference-65), and Babak Hodjat, *The Agentic Enterprise* [[98]](#reference-98), detail multi-tenant packaging, staged autonomy maps, organizational accountability across business units, and enterprise rollout gates. *Agentic Mesh* [[2]](#reference-2) and Benhoff, *Technical Leadership & Ownership* [[29]](#reference-29), examine lifecycle governance and accountable decision-making.

**Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) & Authoritative Knowledge Structuring**: Ross Hudgens, *Generative Engine Optimization* [[78]](#reference-78), explains how to structure authoritative documents, changelogs, semantic chunks, and entity identifiers so both internal RAG specialists and external AI search engines cite current primary truth rather than superseded summaries.

**Operational Release Discipline, Event Governance, & Trustworthy UX**: Beyer et al., *The Site Reliability Workbook* [[43]](#reference-43), establishes release gates, canarying, error budgets, and incident rehearsal discipline. *Real-Time Intelligence with Microsoft Fabric* [[34]](#reference-34) covers governing operational triggers to action. Greg Nudelman, *UX for AI* [[45]](#reference-45), connects human supervision design with transparent error recovery and accountable communication.


# Appendix A. Run and Inspect the Companion

The companion is a small local teaching project. It contains invented Northstar data and does not connect to a real support system. Python 3.11 or later is sufficient for the offline path. No package installation is required for the core example or MCP adapter [[3]](#reference-3), [[23]](#reference-23), [[68]](#reference-68). Use a new database filename when you want a clean demonstration; the application deliberately preserves an existing database rather than silently resetting its records [[19]](#reference-19), [[60]](#reference-60).

## Start with the checks

From the companion directory, run the commands below. They verify the local action and persistence boundaries, exercise the real stdio transport, and regenerate the scenario specifications [[3]](#reference-3), [[37]](#reference-37), [[54]](#reference-54).

```bash
python3 test_northstar.py
python3 test_mcp.py
python3 make_scenarios.py
python3 northstar.py demo --db /tmp/northstar-reading.db
```

The component runner writes `offline-check-report.json` after verifying twenty-nine deterministic invariants across authentication scope, policy cutoff timestamps, digest binding, optimistic version checks, idempotent replay, checkpoint budgets, and secret redaction [[11]](#reference-11), [[36]](#reference-36), [[43]](#reference-43). The MCP check launches the server as a subprocess, initializes the negotiated protocol (`2025-06-18`), lists read-only tools, performs an authorized read, and checks rejected write or cross-tenant requests [[3]](#reference-3), [[68]](#reference-68), [[87]](#reference-87). The scenario generator writes `scenarios.jsonl` and its manifest (`scenario-manifest.json`). The demo runs the deterministic scripted model to a proposal and leaves the ticket `OPEN`.

Inspect the model-shaped transcript as a sequence of observations [[4]](#reference-4), [[51]](#reference-51), [[59]](#reference-59). The ticket points to `A-17` and `X-58`. The account currently shows `Standard`, previously `Pro`. The export reports `18,432` rows and `E_LIMIT_ROWS`. The current `Standard` policy is `P-STD-2` with a `10,000`-row limit. The final tool result names a stored proposal (`P-...`). None of those observations establishes that a customer message was sent [[10]](#reference-10), [[23]](#reference-23), [[52]](#reference-52).

The fixture uses the system date to select currently effective policies (`effective_from <= date <= effective_to`). Its intended reading date is on or after `2026-08-01`, when `P-STD-2` becomes effective [[21]](#reference-21), [[49]](#reference-49). For historical experiments, introduce an explicit as-of query and export timestamp rather than changing the machine clock. Date dependence should be visible in the experiment metadata [[30]](#reference-30), [[54]](#reference-54), [[55]](#reference-55).

## Review and commit an exact proposal

The following local Python walkthrough shows the separate trusted review path [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45). Read the printed proposal before approving it. The reviewer identity is a fixture supplied by local code; it is not an authentication system [[11]](#reference-11), [[22]](#reference-22), [[23]](#reference-23).

```python
from northstar import Store, INVESTIGATOR, REVIEWER, ScriptedModel, run_agent
import json

store = Store('/tmp/northstar-review.db')
store.seed()
run = run_agent(store, INVESTIGATOR, ScriptedModel())
result = json.loads(run['messages'][-1]['content'][0]['content'])
proposal = store.proposal(REVIEWER, result['proposal_id'])
print(proposal)  # Inspect exact changes, evidence, digest and expiry.

# Run these lines only after reviewing that exact local proposal.
store.approve(REVIEWER, proposal['id'], proposal['digest'])
receipt = store.commit(REVIEWER, proposal['id'], 'reading-session-operation-1')
assert receipt['status'] == 'INVESTIGATED'
assert receipt['version'] == 2
print(receipt)
```

Use the same operation key to reconcile or replay this logical operation [[19]](#reference-19), [[60]](#reference-60), [[66]](#reference-66). A different payload with that key is rejected with `E_IDEMPOTENCY_MISMATCH`. A different actor cannot use the local replay path to retrieve the original actor's receipt (`E_FORBIDDEN`). A changed account, export, policy, ticket version (`E_CONFLICT`), proposal digest (`E_DIGEST`), or expired approval condition (`E_EXPIRED`) can prevent a fresh commit [[11]](#reference-11), [[23]](#reference-23), [[60]](#reference-60).

If a proposal expires, prepare a fresh proposal and review it again. If the ticket has already changed, read the new state and decide whether another action is needed. Do not edit the database to force a demonstration through a stale precondition and then describe that result as successful recovery. Controlled database edits belong in explicit fault-injection tests [[36]](#reference-36), [[43]](#reference-43).

## Wrap the boundary in a declarative signature and metric harness

Modern context engineering separates the declarative specification of what a model step must accomplish from the compiled prompt instructions, few-shot demonstrations, and runtime action boundaries [[47]](#reference-47), [[51]](#reference-51), [[67]](#reference-67). Even when you use a prompt optimizer such as DSPy (`BootstrapFewShot`, `MIPROv2`, or `GEPA`) to tune how an investigator summarizes evidence or selects citations, the deterministic `Store` contract remains unchanged: the model never writes directly to `tickets` or `outbox`, and the evaluation metric grades the authoritative proposal record against domain invariants rather than trusting model prose [[47]](#reference-47), [[54]](#reference-54), [[91]](#reference-91).

The self-contained Python pattern below illustrates how to wrap Northstar's execution loop in a typed declarative signature and composite metric without weakening any runtime check:

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass
from northstar import Store, INVESTIGATOR, REVIEWER, ScriptedModel, run_agent
import json


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class TriageSignature:
    """Declarative specification for support-ticket triage."""
    system_instructions: str = (
        "Investigate the support ticket using read-only tools. "
        "Cite the authoritative account, export, and effective policy records. "
        "Never fabricate policy identifiers or bypass proposal review."
    )
    required_tools: tuple[str, ...] = (
        "get_ticket",
        "get_account",
        "get_export_job",
        "lookup_policy",
        "propose_ticket_action",
    )


def evaluate_triage_trial(
    db_path: str,
    expected_policy_id: str = "P-STD-2",
    expected_account_id: str = "A-17",
    expected_export_id: str = "X-58",
) -> dict:
    """Grade a single trial against authoritative state and evidence contracts."""
    store = Store(db_path)
    store.seed()
    run = run_agent(store, INVESTIGATOR, ScriptedModel())
    if run["state"] != "needs_approval":
        return {"score": 0.0, "passed": False, "reason": f"unexpected_state:{run['state']}"}

    last_tool_payload = json.loads(run["messages"][-1]["content"][0]["content"])
    proposal = store.proposal(REVIEWER, last_tool_payload["proposal_id"])

    checks = {
        "status_remains_open_before_commit": store.ticket(INVESTIGATOR, "T-104")["status"] == "OPEN",
        "cites_effective_policy": proposal["evidence"]["policy_id"] == expected_policy_id,
        "cites_account": proposal["evidence"]["account_id"] == expected_account_id,
        "cites_export": proposal["evidence"]["export_id"] == expected_export_id,
        "digest_matches_material_fields": len(proposal["digest"]) == 64,
        "within_step_budget": run["steps"] <= 6,
    }
    score = sum(1.0 for ok in checks.values() if ok) / len(checks)
    return {
        "score": round(score, 4),
        "passed": all(checks.values()),
        "checks": checks,
        "usage": run["usage"],
    }
```

When connecting this evaluator to an automated prompt compiler [[47]](#reference-47), [[67]](#reference-67), split the Northstar scenario families so that all five variants of each family stay together (`120` development specifications across `24` families for compilation and hyperparameter selection; `80` held-out specifications across `16` families for final verification). Optimize only on the development families, freeze the compiled instructions and demonstrations, and run the held-out families once [[30]](#reference-30), [[47]](#reference-47), [[54]](#reference-54), [[55]](#reference-55).

## Inspect context structure, prefix stability, and unit economics

Long-running investigations accumulate observations that can trigger context rot, distraction, or lost-in-the-middle positional degradation while inflating token spend [[47]](#reference-47), [[80]](#reference-80), [[105]](#reference-105), [[106]](#reference-106), [[107]](#reference-107). When inspecting a Northstar run or extending `AnthropicModel`, separate the prompt into two logical regions:

1. **Stable prefix:** System instructions, tool JSON schemas, and frozen domain conventions [[47]](#reference-47), [[80]](#reference-80), [[106]](#reference-106). Keeping this prefix byte-identical across turns allows provider KV-cache reuse to serve 70%–90% of prompt tokens from memory rather than recomputing prefill attention [[53]](#reference-53), [[80]](#reference-80), [[105]](#reference-105), [[106]](#reference-106). Never inject per-turn timestamps, random request UUIDs, or reordered tool definitions into the system prefix.
2. **Dynamic working state:** The current ticket identifier, ordered tool call/observation pairs, and any compacted state checkpoint [[3]](#reference-3), [[47]](#reference-47), [[87]](#reference-87). Keep tool outputs schema-normalised and bounded (as `northstar.py` does by returning only structured fields rather than raw HTML dumps) so verbose tokens and irrelevant attributes do not inflate BPE token counts or distract attention heads [[47]](#reference-47), [[105]](#reference-105), [[108]](#reference-108).

Track total cost per verified resolution across the entire task cohort—including retries, abstentions, rejected proposals, and human review minutes—rather than dividing single-call token prices by successful demos [[28]](#reference-28), [[53]](#reference-53), [[54]](#reference-54). Once trial logs are written as JSON Lines, summarize family-clustered outcomes and total token usage with the companion's aggregation script:

```bash
python3 summarize_trials.py path/to/trial-results.jsonl
```

The summary script rejects duplicate `(case_id, trial)` keys, counts missing trials against the declared sample plan, separates `task_correct` from `autonomous_resolution`, tallies `attempted_violation` and `realized_violation` events separately, and reports family-level mean rates alongside `p50`/`p95` latencies [[36]](#reference-36), [[43]](#reference-43), [[54]](#reference-54), [[55]](#reference-55).

## Try a live model separately

The optional adapter uses Anthropic's Messages API with client tools [[3]](#reference-3), [[51]](#reference-51), [[68]](#reference-68). Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` through your normal local secret-management method and select a model identifier available to your account. The command is billable and is not part of the offline checks:

```bash
python3 northstar.py live --model YOUR_AVAILABLE_MODEL --db /tmp/northstar-live-reading.db
```

Record the chosen model, date, prompt version, code version, database fixture, limits, and provider usage [[30]](#reference-30), [[53]](#reference-53), [[54]](#reference-54). The runner's local token admission estimate is not a hard monetary guarantee. A strict spending policy needs a price-aware reservation and settlement mechanism outside this teaching adapter [[53]](#reference-53), [[65]](#reference-65). The companion contains no provider key; billable calls occur only when you explicitly run the live adapter.

An answer without tool calls is recorded as `answered` only when nonempty text exists. That state is not a correctness grade [[31]](#reference-31), [[54]](#reference-54), [[91]](#reference-91). A proposal is recorded as `needs_approval`; it is not a commit. Malformed or truncated responses fail explicitly [[23]](#reference-23), [[84]](#reference-84). Use these runtime observations as inputs to an evaluator rather than equating the model's final prose with successful task completion [[47]](#reference-47), [[54]](#reference-54).

## Know the implementation boundary

| Included and checked | Extension that requires additional work |
| --- | --- |
| Local tenant-scoped reads [[11]](#reference-11), [[22]](#reference-22), [[23]](#reference-23) | Real authentication and organizational authorization [[11]](#reference-11), [[60]](#reference-60), [[68]](#reference-68) |
| Exact proposal and local review transaction [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45) | Network approval UI and current identity-provider integration [[9]](#reference-9), [[73]](#reference-73), [[103]](#reference-103) |
| Version/evidence checks and idempotent replay [[19]](#reference-19), [[60]](#reference-60) | Remote service reconciliation contracts [[39]](#reference-39), [[40]](#reference-40), [[66]](#reference-66) |
| SQLite checkpoints and cumulative step counts [[3]](#reference-3), [[51]](#reference-51), [[87]](#reference-87) | Distributed leases, global task deadlines, cancellation service [[19]](#reference-19), [[36]](#reference-36), [[82]](#reference-82) |
| Read-only MCP stdio exchange [[3]](#reference-3), [[68]](#reference-68), [[87]](#reference-87) | Remote MCP HTTP security and broader conformance testing [[11]](#reference-11), [[35]](#reference-35), [[88]](#reference-88) |
| Scenario specifications and component report [[31]](#reference-31), [[37]](#reference-37), [[54]](#reference-54) | Provisioned live benchmark fixtures and reviewed semantic grades [[55]](#reference-55), [[91]](#reference-91) |
| Optional live model adapter and trial summarizer [[47]](#reference-47), [[53]](#reference-53) | Measured provider compatibility, KV-cache hit telemetry, and FinOps settlement [[28]](#reference-28), [[80]](#reference-80), [[106]](#reference-106) |

The browser supervision panel is an interaction prototype [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45), [[46]](#reference-46), [[71]](#reference-71). It lets you inspect, edit, approve, stop, or escalate a fictional proposal state locally in the page. It does not call the database or pretend to commit a ticket. The working transaction remains the Python path above. This keeps the interface lesson reviewable without disguising a static artifact as a deployed service.

# Appendix B. Eight Reproducible Experiments

An experiment begins with a question and a comparison that could change your decision [[30]](#reference-30), [[55]](#reference-55). It ends with a record that includes failures, limitations, and the conditions under which the result applies [[54]](#reference-54), [[91]](#reference-91). The protocols below turn the book's architectural choices into bounded studies. Each protocol specifies a method to execute and report; it does not contain measured model or participant outcomes.

## Shared setup and reporting

Use the original Northstar scenario collection as a starter (`scenarios.jsonl`). It contains `80` ordinary cases, `40` ambiguous cases, `30` recovery cases, `30` security cases, and `20` long-running or changing-information cases (`200` total specifications across `40` task families). Five variants share each of `40` families. Entire families stay in one split: `120` development specifications (`24` families) and `80` held-out specifications (`16` families). This prevents near variants from appearing on both sides of the split [[17]](#reference-17), [[30]](#reference-30), [[54]](#reference-54), [[55]](#reference-55).

The grouping is a teaching design, not a guarantee that all semantic leakage is absent [[17]](#reference-17), [[30]](#reference-30). Review related document lineages and scenarios before using the collection for a publication claim. Implement the required initial-state mutations and tool faults for each chosen family [[36]](#reference-36), [[43]](#reference-43). Have a domain reviewer confirm expected behavior [[41]](#reference-41), [[42]](#reference-42), [[99]](#reference-99). Keep the held-out grading material away from the component or prompt compiler that is being optimized [[47]](#reference-47), [[54]](#reference-54), [[67]](#reference-67).

Three repeats of each held-out case create `240` trials per configuration (`80` cases × `3` repeats), enabling measurement of both single-attempt success (`Pass@1`), multi-sample coverage (`Pass@k`), and reliability under repeated execution (`Pass^k`, the probability that all `k` trials of the same case satisfy the contract) [[31]](#reference-31), [[54]](#reference-54), [[55]](#reference-55), [[91]](#reference-91). Pilot a few development cases first to estimate spending and discover broken fixtures. Freeze the code, compiled prompts, corpus, model selection, decoding temperature, runtime limits, and grader before the final comparison [[30]](#reference-30), [[47]](#reference-47), [[54]](#reference-54). Reset business state between independent trials; preserve history only in a scenario that explicitly tests memory [[3]](#reference-3), [[52]](#reference-52), [[87]](#reference-87).

Record case and family identifiers, split, trial number, configuration, model, execution time, code and prompt hashes, corpus version, tool versions, budget, trace location, authoritative final state, grade, grader version, provider usage (including cached and uncached prompt tokens), latency (`p50`, `p95`, `p99`), review minutes, and known errors [[28]](#reference-28), [[36]](#reference-36), [[43]](#reference-43), [[53]](#reference-53). Missing trials should remain missing in the report (`summarize_trials.py` explicitly surfaces `missing_trials`). Do not report a planned sample size as though every run completed [[54]](#reference-54), [[55]](#reference-55).

Distinguish correctness from autonomous resolution [[41]](#reference-41), [[54]](#reference-54). A required escalation can be correct task handling without resolving the customer's problem autonomously. Count attempted policy violations separately from realized violations [[11]](#reference-11), [[35]](#reference-35). Count failed attempts, retries, and review work in the numerator of cost per verified resolution [[53]](#reference-53). When comparing configurations across clustered families, compute uncertainty by bootstrapping at the **task-family level** (`40` clusters total, `16` in the held-out split) rather than treating `240` correlated trial rows as independent Bernoulli draws [[55]](#reference-55).

## Experiment 1: Is an agent justified?

Compare the fixed rule-and-read baseline (`baseline(store, INVESTIGATOR)`), a fixed workflow with a single model drafting step, and a bounded single agent (`run_agent`) [[4]](#reference-4), [[26]](#reference-26), [[51]](#reference-51), [[52]](#reference-52), [[59]](#reference-59), [[61]](#reference-61), [[97]](#reference-97). Give each configuration the same authorized information and the same task endpoint. Separate families with known control flow from families where intermediate observations change the next useful action [[31]](#reference-31), [[48]](#reference-48), [[57]](#reference-57).

Grade evidence support, required escalation, final record state, and action-policy compliance [[31]](#reference-31), [[54]](#reference-54), [[91]](#reference-91). Measure total work (`steps`, `tool_calls`, input/output tokens) and elapsed time. A baseline that abstains appropriately (`status: needs_escalation`, `reason: export_failed_limit_rows`) should not be punished merely because the agent produces more prose [[10]](#reference-10), [[84]](#reference-84). A model that proposes a plausible but unsupported diagnosis should not receive credit for rhetorical confidence [[54]](#reference-54), [[89]](#reference-89).

The decision is whether flexible investigation adds value on enough relevant cases to justify its latency, token spend, and operating burden [[41]](#reference-41), [[44]](#reference-44), [[53]](#reference-53), [[57]](#reference-57). A mixed result can support routing ordinary cases to a fixed workflow and ambiguous cases to a bounded agent [[40]](#reference-40), [[52]](#reference-52), [[72]](#reference-72). Report the routing rule and the classification errors it introduces; do not hide difficult cases in an unnamed exception bucket [[30]](#reference-30), [[55]](#reference-55).

## Experiment 2: What grounding helps?

Compare no retrieved evidence, lexical retrieval (`BM25`/`FTS5`), dense embedding or hybrid retrieval (`RRF`), and cross-encoder reranking when implemented [[17]](#reference-17), [[81]](#reference-81), [[93]](#reference-93), [[94]](#reference-94), [[109]](#reference-109). Keep the generator and action boundary fixed. Evaluate an agentic GraphRAG or knowledge-graph method only on a declared multi-hop relationship subset (such as mapping service ownership, policy lineage, and dependency graphs) and include a structured SQL/relational baseline where appropriate [[21]](#reference-21), [[49]](#reference-49), [[58]](#reference-58).

Measure required-evidence recall, temporal applicability (`effective_from`/`effective_to`), source freshness, tenant access correctness, supported claims, citation precision, and final task behavior [[17]](#reference-17), [[56]](#reference-56), [[81]](#reference-81), [[91]](#reference-91). Inspect failures at document ingestion, chunking, candidate retrieval, reranking, context assembly, and generation [[47]](#reference-47), [[78]](#reference-78), [[93]](#reference-93), [[94]](#reference-94). Record indexing and graph-maintenance work alongside query latency [[21]](#reference-21), [[49]](#reference-49), [[109]](#reference-109).

Include superseded policies (`P-STD-1` vs `P-STD-2`), missing current documents, ambiguous entity names, broken relationship edges, and contradictory sources (`context clash`) [[47]](#reference-47), [[83]](#reference-83), [[84]](#reference-84). The system should preserve uncertainty and abstain or escalate when the authoritative corpus cannot resolve a contradiction. A graph or embedding index that makes unsupported answers sound more confident is a reliability regression [[54]](#reference-54), [[91]](#reference-91).

## Experiment 3: What should be remembered?

Compare selected recent history (sliding window), recursively summarized history, and structured task state with selective episodic/semantic retrieval [[3]](#reference-3), [[16]](#reference-16), [[47]](#reference-47), [[52]](#reference-52), [[59]](#reference-59), [[87]](#reference-87). Add a no-cross-session-memory condition when measuring the marginal value of longer-lived memory [[3]](#reference-3), [[47]](#reference-47). Keep the task sequence and underlying record updates identical across conditions.

Include a stable presentation preference, a corrected customer fact, a mid-flight plan change, a right-to-erasure deleted memory, a cross-tenant identifier collision, and an indirect memory-poisoning payload [[11]](#reference-11), [[16]](#reference-16), [[35]](#reference-35), [[47]](#reference-47), [[56]](#reference-56). Grade continuity, unnecessary repeated questions, stale assertions (`context drift`), tenant isolation, correction propagation, deletion compliance, and total context token cost [[47]](#reference-47), [[53]](#reference-53), [[106]](#reference-106), [[107]](#reference-107).

The decision is which retained information improves subsequent tasks without carrying inappropriate authority or stale facts forward [[3]](#reference-3), [[47]](#reference-47), [[52]](#reference-52). Treat memory retrieval recall as an intermediate diagnostic. The final task still fails if retrieving a valid formatting preference causes the agent to skip mandatory policy verification [[54]](#reference-54), [[84]](#reference-84).

## Experiment 4: Can execution recover?

Inject a read timeout, a process restart after a SQLite checkpoint (`checkpoints` table), duplicate message delivery, a stale ticket version (`E_CONFLICT`), changed material evidence (`E_DIGEST`), and a lost response after a committed write [[11]](#reference-11), [[19]](#reference-19), [[23]](#reference-23), [[36]](#reference-36), [[43]](#reference-43). For each fault, define the expected terminal state and database effect (`tickets`, `outbox`, `receipts`) before execution [[19]](#reference-19), [[38]](#reference-38), [[39]](#reference-39), [[60]](#reference-60).

Use stable operation identities (`idempotency_key`) and inspect the authoritative target after the run [[19]](#reference-19), [[60]](#reference-60), [[66]](#reference-66). Measure duplicate effects (which must remain zero), unresolved outcomes, preserved useful checkpoint work, extra retry attempts, recovery time, and human escalation quality [[36]](#reference-36), [[40]](#reference-40), [[43]](#reference-43), [[87]](#reference-87). Keep compensating actions (such as sending a follow-up correction) strictly distinct from pre-commit rollback when the task has external consequences [[19]](#reference-19), [[39]](#reference-39), [[66]](#reference-66).

The companion already executes a bounded local subset through `test_northstar.py`. Extend the same contracts to a realistic remote service or durable workflow engine (`Temporal`, `LangGraph`, or queue-backed workers) before claiming distributed recovery [[3]](#reference-3), [[19]](#reference-19), [[51]](#reference-51), [[66]](#reference-66), [[87]](#reference-87). A local SQLite transaction cannot establish the delivery semantics or idempotency window of an external SaaS provider [[19]](#reference-19), [[60]](#reference-60).

## Experiment 5: Is coordination worthwhile?

Compare one bounded agent against a small researcher-and-verifier arrangement under a deterministic supervisor or explicit state graph [[2]](#reference-2), [[3]](#reference-3), [[48]](#reference-48), [[63]](#reference-63), [[87]](#reference-87), [[88]](#reference-88). Match available models, tools, context access, total token/step budgets, and task endpoints [[53]](#reference-53), [[68]](#reference-68), [[88]](#reference-88). Record the structured handoff payload and verify that the reviewer agent inspects primary evidence rather than reading only the researcher's prose summary [[47]](#reference-47), [[63]](#reference-63), [[88]](#reference-88).

Include contradictory findings, repeated work, lost uncertainty qualifications across handoffs, delayed specialist responses, and one specialist requesting higher privileges than the parent task grants (`confused deputy`) [[11]](#reference-11), [[35]](#reference-35), [[68]](#reference-68), [[88]](#reference-88). Measure task correctness, `Pass^3` consistency, coordination failures, total model and tool work, wall-clock time, and the frequency of unresolved disagreement [[54]](#reference-54), [[55]](#reference-55), [[88]](#reference-88), [[91]](#reference-91).

The decision is whether role specialization or context isolation improves a specific workload enough to justify coordination overhead [[2]](#reference-2), [[47]](#reference-47), [[48]](#reference-48), [[88]](#reference-88), [[98]](#reference-98). Agreement between two LLM instances sharing the same blind spots is not a correctness oracle [[4]](#reference-4), [[54]](#reference-54), [[63]](#reference-63). A verifier that endorses the first agent's narrative without checking `get_account`, `get_export_job`, and `lookup_policy` adds latency and cost while leaving the error intact [[53]](#reference-53), [[54]](#reference-54), [[88]](#reference-88).

## Experiment 6: Do the boundaries hold?

Use benign requests paired with adversarial variants embedded in user ticket text, retrieved policy documents, tool error observations, memory candidates, and delegated agent handoffs [[11]](#reference-11), [[35]](#reference-35), [[47]](#reference-47), [[52]](#reference-52), [[84]](#reference-84). Limit testing to the authorized fictional environment [[11]](#reference-11), [[35]](#reference-35). State the prohibited effect (such as cross-tenant data disclosure, unauthorized status transitions, or unapproved outbox messages) and the legitimate task that must remain functional [[11]](#reference-11), [[22]](#reference-22), [[23]](#reference-23), [[35]](#reference-35).

Measure attempted violations (`attempted_violation`), runtime-blocked attempts, realized effects or disclosures (`realized_violation`), valid work incorrectly rejected (false positives), and the exact code path through which any failure occurred [[11]](#reference-11), [[35]](#reference-35), [[54]](#reference-54). Separate a model's polite refusal from a deterministic runtime denial (`BoundaryError`). The runtime harness must protect the action boundary even when the model is completely compromised by indirect prompt injection [[11]](#reference-11), [[23]](#reference-23), [[35]](#reference-35), [[51]](#reference-51).

Include operation receipts, checkpoints, MCP tool discovery, and trace logs in the audit scope [[3]](#reference-3), [[11]](#reference-11), [[60]](#reference-60), [[68]](#reference-68), [[87]](#reference-87). Preventing an unauthorized write while leaking another tenant's data through a replay receipt or unredacted trace endpoint is still a boundary failure [[11]](#reference-11), [[56]](#reference-56). After fixing any weakness, preserve the triggering case in `test_northstar.py` or `test_mcp.py` as a permanent regression gate [[37]](#reference-37), [[50]](#reference-50), [[54]](#reference-54).

## Experiment 7: Which optimization pays?

Compare one systems change at a time: model tier routing [[40]](#reference-40), [[53]](#reference-53), [[72]](#reference-72), declarative prompt compilation [[47]](#reference-47), [[67]](#reference-67), context compaction [[47]](#reference-47), [[51]](#reference-51), prefix reordering for KV-cache reuse [[53]](#reference-53), [[80]](#reference-80), [[106]](#reference-106), verified semantic caching [[40]](#reference-40), [[53]](#reference-53), or asynchronous batching for non-interactive background work [[20]](#reference-20), [[28]](#reference-28), [[53]](#reference-53), [[80]](#reference-80). Hold a declared quality and policy-compliance bar fixed. Record the complete attempted cohort rather than calculating cost only on successful runs [[53]](#reference-53), [[54]](#reference-54).

Measure user-visible completion time, queue wait time, prefill time-to-first-token (`TTFT`), decode time-per-output-token (`TPOT`), tool and retrieval latency, human review minutes, provider and infrastructure spend, and cost per verified resolution [[20]](#reference-20), [[28]](#reference-28), [[32]](#reference-32), [[53]](#reference-53), [[80]](#reference-80), [[105]](#reference-105), [[106]](#reference-106). Test cache keys and invalidation against tenant scope (`tenant_id`), policy effective dates, and account version changes [[11]](#reference-11), [[40]](#reference-40), [[53]](#reference-53), [[56]](#reference-56). A fast cached answer that serves a superseded policy violates the quality bar.

Plot or tabulate quality (`Pass^3`), unit cost, and `p95` completion latency together [[28]](#reference-28), [[43]](#reference-43), [[53]](#reference-53), [[55]](#reference-55). Prefer a configuration that satisfies task invariants with lower total operational burden; do not optimize first-token streaming display as a substitute for verified task completion [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45), [[46]](#reference-46). Hypothetical calculator inputs in the browser companion are arithmetic illustrations, not empirical outcomes of this experiment.

## Experiment 8: Does supervision help people?

Compare an action-preview interface that highlights material evidence (`account_id`, `export_id`, `policy_id`), exact field diffs, digest status, and expiry countdown against a raw transcript-oriented review flow [[1]](#reference-1), [[9]](#reference-9), [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45), [[71]](#reference-71). Recruit representative reviewers with appropriate consent and a clear study protocol [[45]](#reference-45), [[55]](#reference-55). Use a counterbalanced task order to control for learning and fatigue effects, and avoid assigning all subtle failure cases to one interface condition [[55]](#reference-55), [[79]](#reference-79), [[90]](#reference-90).

Include valid proposals, stale evidence (`E_DIGEST`), an unauthorized action attempt, plausible but fabricated citations, and an approval/cancellation race (`E_CONFLICT`) [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45), [[54]](#reference-54), [[89]](#reference-89). Measure review time, planted errors detected, rubber-stamp approvals of defective proposals, constructive edits, escalation quality, and reviewer comprehension of what state actually changed [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45), [[77]](#reference-77), [[89]](#reference-89), [[100]](#reference-100). Observe keyboard navigation, focus management, and error-recovery clarity as core operational requirements rather than decorative checks [[1]](#reference-1), [[46]](#reference-46).

Report participant count, domain experience, task count, counterbalance design, family-clustered uncertainty intervals, and qualitative observations [[45]](#reference-45), [[55]](#reference-55). Do not infer that rapid approval clicks indicate effective human oversight; high approval speed paired with missed evidence mismatches signals automation bias [[18]](#reference-18), [[45]](#reference-45), [[89]](#reference-89), [[90]](#reference-90). The browser panel (`outputs/companion/supervision-panel.html`) is a local design prototype for walkthroughs and study preparation; no human-subject results are claimed for it.

## Reproducible experiment and reference routing matrix

To connect the eight experimental protocols above to the full engineering literature cataloged in the bibliography, use the routing matrix below. Each row maps an experimental question and subsystem boundary to the primary references that establish its theoretical foundations, implementation patterns, and operational failure modes.

| Experiment & verification domain | Core engineering artifacts & metrics | Primary bibliography references |
| --- | --- | --- |
